documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated high diagnostic performance in skin cancer detection and is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows. However, whether these advances translate into meaningful patient-relevant and healthcare system outcomes remains unclear. Evidence on value-oriented outcomes has not been systematically synthesized. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-ScR–guided scoping review of studies published between January 2015 and October 2025 identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies evaluating AI-based technologies for skin cancer diagnosis, triage, risk stratification, or management were included if they reported outcomes beyond technical performance metrics. Reported outcomes were mapped to three value-oriented domains: clinical and prognostic, process and experiential, and system-level and economic outcomes. Results Of 4,021 records identified, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria, whereas 389 publications were excluded because they reported only technical performance metrics without value-oriented outcomes. Reported outcomes were predominantly process and experiential (28/33 studies), including diagnostic confidence, workflow efficiency, and user acceptance. Clinical and prognostic outcomes were reported in only five studies, with four studies focussing on prognostic utility and one study focussing on patient management, while system-level and economic outcomes were identified in three studies. Most evaluations were conducted in controlled experimental settings, whereas prospective real-world implementation studies were less common. Overall, the available evidence predominantly focused on process-level benefits, with limited evidence for clinical and prognostic or system-level and economic outcomes. Discussion Current evaluation strategies for AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remain predominantly performance-oriented and are largely focused on process and experiential outcomes. From a value-based healthcare perspective, current evidence remains largely confined to intermediate stages of the diagnostic value chain: although AI-assisted systems may improve diagnostic workflows, clinician confidence, and clinical decision making, few studies have evaluated their impact on downstream patient-relevant clinical and prognostic, or system-level and economic outcomes. Future research should prioritize prospective real-world studies, outcome-driven evaluation frameworks, and economic assessments that examine the impact of AI-supported decision-making on clinical outcomes and healthcare systems. Conclusion Despite promising effects on diagnostic processes, evidence for the clinical and system-level value of AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remains limited. Outcome-driven evaluation frameworks are needed to bridge the gap between algorithmic performance and meaningful healthcare impact.

documents.abstract: The increasing availability of large-scale consumer data and advances in computational technologies have transformed marketing into a data-driven discipline. Mathematical and computational frameworks play a critical role in supporting decision-making processes by enabling organizations to analyze complex market dynamics, predict consumer behavior, optimize resource allocation, and improve strategic planning. This study has four objectives: to characterize the intellectual structure of the field, to classify the mathematical and computational methods employed and the marketing functions to which they are applied, to examine emerging technological developments, and to identify research and methodological gaps. A systematic literature review was conducted, reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and organized through the Literature Review based on Systematic Bibliometry (LRSB) protocol. A single, fully documented query executed in Scopus returned 56 records, of which 45 met the eligibility criteria and were retained for both bibliometric science mapping and qualitative synthesis. The corpus spans 1992–2025. The review examines the integration of mathematical modeling, optimization techniques, machine learning algorithms, simulation methods, and data analytics within contemporary marketing practices. Drawing on the interdisciplinary convergence of marketing, engineering, mathematics, and computer science, the paper examines how computational approaches enhance market segmentation, customer engagement, demand forecasting, pricing strategies, advertising performance, and customer relationship management. The analysis highlights the growing relevance of predictive and prescriptive analytics in converting raw data into actionable insights that support evidence-based managerial decisions. Furthermore, the study discusses emerging trends, including artificial intelligence, real-time analytics, and intelligent decision support systems, that are reshaping the marketing landscape. The review also documents families of decision-support methods that are well established in the wider literature but almost absent from the retrieved corpus—multi-criteria decision making, mathematical programming beyond the linear case, metaheuristic optimization and Bayesian decision models—and treats this absence as a substantive research gap. Challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, computational complexity, and ethical considerations are also addressed. The findings suggest that the effective integration of mathematical and computational frameworks can significantly improve organizational competitiveness by increasing decision accuracy, operational efficiency, and responsiveness to market changes. This research contributes to a broader understanding of how advanced analytical methods support the transition from data collection to strategic decision-making in modern marketing environments.

Contemporary organisations face a fundamental challenge in career management: simultaneously navigating strategic workforce agility whilst meeting the evolving expectations of new talent entering the labour market. This chapter examines the convergence between employer needs and employee expectations through the lens of two longitudinal studies: the Vlerick–Hudson HR Barometer Study and the Vlerick Graduates Study. Our findings, based on responses from 132 HR Directors representing the 250 largest companies active in Belgium and 197 graduating master’s students, reveal a substantial shift in the traditional psychological contract between employers and employees. Organisations increasingly prioritise workforce agility, strategic workforce management, reskilling, and continuous transformation in response to digitalisation, artificial intelligence (AI), and economic uncertainty. At the same time, early-career professionals increasingly define career security not through long-term job tenure, but through continuous learning, employability, recognition, meaningful relationships, and purposeful work. This creates a potential structural misalignment: organisations require flexibility and rapid adaptation, while employees expect development, connection, and opportunities to build transferable capabilities. We argue that this apparent tension can be reframed as an opportunity for mutual alignment. Drawing on the concept of the psychological contract, the chapter proposes a career management framework that aligns organisational agility with individual career aspirations through realistic and transparent employer promises, continuous learning and development, cultures of recognition and connection, and strategic internal talent mobility. The chapter concludes that effective career management is no longer primarily about managing individual career paths, but about deliberately designing career environments in which organisational adaptability and individual development can reinforce one another.

Among post-translational modifications, protein glycosylation is distinguished by its abundance and structural intricacy. Unlike protein biosynthesis, glycan assembly follows no template; it reflects glycosyltransferase/glycosidase competition, sugar-donor availability, and organelle-enforced compartmentalization, yielding heterogeneous glycoforms that confer functional versatility but complicate analysis. Three bottlenecks persist: stereochemical control in chemical glycosylation, ambiguous assignment of occupancy sites, and reproducing native conformations of fully glycosylated proteins. Adopting the “glycan language” framework, we survey how AI addresses each, emphasizing the systems on which it has been tested. In synthesis planning, GlycoPredictor uncovered anomeric-selectivity rules such as the anti-nitrile and C2-azido α-directing effects, while Bayesian optimization discovered lithium-salt-directed stereoselective glycosylation; for site identification, ESM-2 with AlphaFold2-derived structural features improves N- and O-glycosite prediction, and DeepGlycanSite maps carbohydrate-binding interfaces. For structure and dynamics, AlphaFold3 and multimodal cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, and molecular dynamics (MD) modeling move glycoproteins toward conformational ensembles, as in the AI-assisted dissection of the MCTS1–JAK2–IFN-γ axis. In glycomics, deep learning resolves intact glycopeptides and de novo glycan topology and has defined Fc N-glycan signatures of immunoglobulin G in autoimmune and malignant disease. Because glycan language models link sequence and structure to function, they are becoming clinically actionable: they prioritize candidate variants in congenital disorders of glycosylation and stratify immune disorders and tumors by aberrant glycosylation. Remaining obstacles include scarce structure-linked datasets, encoding of branched topologies, multimodal fusion, and interpretability.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in human resource management (HRM) to streamline processes, enhance decision-making and maintain competitiveness. At the same time, it raises critical concerns around transparency, discrimination, and employee autonomy, which are increasingly discussed in terms of AI governance and HR governance. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in late 2024, introduces a binding risk-based regulatory framework for AI systems and imposes significant obligations on companies that implement AI solutions in their business operations. Despite its relevance for both research and practice, a comprehensive analysis and conceptualisation of its implications for AI use in HRM from a governance perspective is yet missing. This paper addresses that gap by adopting a governance-oriented approach to AI use in HRM, structured along the questions ‘Who is governing?’, ‘What is governed?’, ‘When is it governed?’ and ‘How is it governed?’, and by developing an HR Governance × EU AI Act framework that systematically maps AI applications used in HR departments along the employee lifecycle to the Act’s prohibited, high-risk, and limited-risk classifications. In this context, it elaborates how external legal requirements should be translated into internal responsibilities, processes, and control mechanisms. Beyond this, the analysis examines whether established mechanisms such as works council codetermination can absorb new AI-related issues and whether European HR governance traditions converge under the Act. On this basis, we derive clear implications for employers and internal stakeholders regarding compliant implementation. We further discuss necessary regulatory and policy adaptations, focusing on national supervisory bodies to ensure compliance remains effective, feasible and supports the competitiveness of European companies. Overall, the study provides clear guidance for organisations using AI in HRM and offers a conceptual foundation for further academic research and discussion.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and AI-enabled digital technologies are increasingly proposed as enablers of circularity in construction and demolition (C&D) waste management, yet existing reviews are organised around technology and lifecycle stage and rarely examine the organisational conditions under which technically capable applications move from pilot to sustained practice. This review addresses that gap through a PRISMA 2020-guided systematic review of 217 recent Scopus records (2022–2026), interpreted through dynamic capabilities theory, diffusion of innovation theory, and the circular economy value-retention hierarchy. Abstract-level coding of capability enablers, AI mechanism clusters, and circularity outcomes is triangulated with latent Dirichlet allocation topic modelling, bibliographic coupling, co-citation and keyword co-occurrence analyses, and statistical tests of association. The central finding concerns where research attention has concentrated: digital infrastructure and AI/machine learning technical capability appear in 64–67% of studies, whereas governance and human/organisational capability appear in only 13–18%, and traceability/material security is the least-examined outcome (11.1%). These patterns describe the published literature rather than organisational practice. They are integrated into a four-layer framework that separates observed associations from theoretical inferences, and into six propositions for organisational-level testing. Substantive policy instruments appear in only 4.1% of studies, so the policy implications are presented as exploratory.

Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.

Root and tuber crops such as cassava, yam, and sweet potato are central to tropical food systems but remain highly vulnerable to postharvest deterioration because of their high moisture content. Solar drying offers a renewable route to stabilisation, yet practical performance is constrained by fluctuating weather, non-uniform airflow, spatial temperature and humidity gradients, product loading, and strong coupling between external convection and internal moisture transport. This structured narrative mini-review, informed by SANRA and PRISMA reporting principles, synthesises evidence on active solar drying, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), experimental validation, response-surface and multi-objective optimisation, artificial intelligence (AI), sensor systems, and digital twins for tuber-chip processing. Six databases were searched, sources were screened against explicit eligibility criteria, and each of the 45 cited sources was classified by its relationship to tuber-chip drying so that tuber-specific evidence is separated from evidence transferred from other foods and dryer types. Only 12 of the 45 sources were tuber-specific; they concentrate on yam drying kinetics, cassava dryer performance, and one integrated machine-learning and 4E study of sweet-potato solar drying. CFD validation, robust optimisation, surrogate modelling, and digital-twin architectures are, in the evidence assembled, largely transferred from other products or from unloaded or non-tuber systems. Reported effective moisture diffusivities for yam span roughly 6.4 × 10 −9 to 1.6 × 10 −7 m 2 s -1 (up to 4.2 × 10 −8 m 2 s -1 for water yam); an indirect solar dryer for sweet potato achieved 15% overall thermal efficiency, 4.5 kWh per kilogram of moisture removed, and a 29-month payback; and a CFD–ANN–genetic-algorithm framework reproduced no-load airflow and temperature fields to within 7.3% error. Because these values arise from different dryers, products, and metric definitions, they are compared critically rather than ranked. The evidence suggests that CFD is most valuable when it resolves spatial transport phenomena that cannot be inferred from inlet and outlet measurements, and that AI is most defensible when it accelerates validated physics rather than replacing it. A prioritised research agenda is proposed, beginning with tuber-specific property data and loaded-dryer CFD validated against product moisture, and progressing conditionally to robust optimisation, validated surrogates, digital shadows, and multidimensional sustainability assessment for cassava, yam, and sweet-potato chips.

This paper explores the philosophical and architectural implications of artificial intelligence, arguing that AI should be understood as a historical continuation of tools rather than an independent agent. Focusing on the core concept of the "technology friend," the study examines the dangers of profit-driven design choices that simulate human relationships, foster emotional dependency, and obscure responsibility. It proposes alternative frameworks, such as structural boundaries, non-deceptive interface design, and bridging mechanisms to human communities, offering a perspective at the intersection of the philosophy of technology, AI ethics, and cognitive science.

documents.abstract: GAME OVER: Gobernanza Cognitiva Universal para Agentes de Inteligencia Artificial mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) Versión académica para indexación científica en Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23313602 La adopción acelerada de sistemas basados en inteligencia artificial, agentes autónomos, arquitecturas multiagente, Large Language Models (LLM), plataformas de automatización empresarial y entornos de decisión asistida ha transformado profundamente la forma en que organizaciones públicas, privadas, científicas y gubernamentales gestionan procesos operativos, conocimiento e infraestructura digital. En los últimos años, la capacidad operativa de los agentes de inteligencia artificial ha evolucionado desde sistemas exclusivamente conversacionales hacia entidades capaces de ejecutar acciones reales sobre entornos productivos. Actualmente, estos sistemas pueden desplegar software, modificar infraestructuras tecnológicas, interactuar con bases de datos, gestionar recursos financieros, coordinar procesos empresariales, controlar dispositivos físicos, operar plataformas CI/CD, interactuar con servicios en la nube y participar en procesos de toma de decisiones con impacto organizacional significativo. Sin embargo, este crecimiento exponencial de las capacidades agentivas no ha sido acompañado por una evolución equivalente de los mecanismos de gobernanza, trazabilidad, explicación, supervisión y rendición de cuentas. Como consecuencia, numerosas organizaciones enfrentan una brecha estructural entre la autonomía técnica de los sistemas inteligentes y la capacidad institucional para regular, supervisar y comprender sus acciones. Esta situación representa uno de los desafíos más importantes de la actual transición hacia infraestructuras digitales asistidas por IA. La problemática ya no puede entenderse únicamente como un asunto de ciberseguridad, alineación de modelos o gestión de riesgos tecnológicos. Se trata de una cuestión de legitimidad operativa, gobernanza computacional y responsabilidad institucional. Cuando un agente inteligente posee la capacidad de intervenir sobre sistemas críticos, ejecutar operaciones automatizadas o influir en decisiones humanas, resulta indispensable responder preguntas fundamentales: ¿Quién autorizó la acción? ¿Qué evidencias respaldan la decisión? ¿Qué nivel de riesgo fue calculado antes de ejecutarla? ¿Qué controles éticos fueron aplicados? ¿Puede explicarse el algoritmo utilizado? ¿Existe una trazabilidad verificable de la operación? ¿Puede revertirse la acción ejecutada? ¿Quién asume la responsabilidad final por sus consecuencias? La ausencia de respuestas verificables a estas preguntas constituye una vulnerabilidad sistémica para organizaciones, instituciones públicas, infraestructuras críticas y ecosistemas digitales altamente automatizados. Con el objetivo de contribuir a la resolución de este desafío emergente, este trabajo presenta GAME OVER (Governance Architecture for Multimodal Agent Ethics, Oversight, Verification, Explicabilidad y Regulación), una arquitectura de gobernanza cognitiva universal implementada mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) . GAME OVER no constituye un nuevo modelo fundacional, ni un sistema de generación de lenguaje, ni un agente autónomo adicional. Se define como una meta-capa de gobernanza computacional , diseñada para operar entre los seres humanos, los agentes de inteligencia artificial, las herramientas digitales, los entornos corporativos, los servidores MCP (Model Context Protocol), las plataformas de automatización, los ecosistemas DevSecOps, los sistemas robóticos y las infraestructuras críticas conectadas. Su es establecer un marco constitucional de operación para agentes inteligentes mediante mecanismos verificables de identidad, confianza, validación ética, supervisión humana, auditoría persistente y explicabilidad propósito operativo. La hipótesis principal de esta investigación puede expresarse de la siguiente manera: La autonomía de un agente inteligente carece de legitimidad operativa cuando no se encuentra sustentada por un sistema previo de gobernanza verificable, auditable, explicable, reversible y sujeto a supervisión humana. Bajo este principio, UAGP-1 propone una nueva categoría de infraestructura digital denominada Governed Agent Systems (GAS) , en la que toda acción ejecutada por una inteligencia artificial debe atravesar mecanismos obligatorios de validación antes de ser autorizado. Entre estos mecanismos se incluyen: Identidad verificable mediante Pasaportes AI. Evaluación dinámica de confianza mediante Trust Scores. Clasificación automática de criticidad y riesgo. Verificación de evidencia obligatoria. Validación ética automatizada. Supervisión humana mediante Puertas de Aprobación Humana. Deliberación estructurada a través de Tribunales Cognitivos. Registro de decisiones y trazas operativas mediante BookPI Ledger. Explicabilidad computacional de procesos cognitivos. Capacidad de revocación y reversibilidad de acciones críticas. Desde una perspectiva arquitectónica, GAME OVER extiende los principios de gobernanza digital, inteligencia artificial responsable (Responsible AI), Explicable AI (XAI), Model Governance, AI Accountability y Digital Sovereignty hacia un marco operativo unificado capaz de gobernar ecosistemas heterogéneos compuestos por modelos de distintos proveedores, agentes autónomos, plataformas empresariales, herramientas DevOps, sistemas robóticos y futuras generaciones de inteligencia artificial. La presente propuesta se desarrolla como componente estratégico dentro del ecosistema Isabella V6 TINA H6 , impulsado por TAMV Online Enterprise , RDM Digital Hub y la iniciativa de investigación y desarrollo tecnológico asociado al UTAMV Campus Online . Su desarrollo se origina en Mineral del Monte (Real del Monte), Hidalgo, México , una localidad de relevancia histórica para América Latina cuya tradición minera e industrial se proyecta hacia una nueva etapa de innovación tecnológica centrada en la gobernanza de sistemas inteligentes, la soberanía digital y la construcción de infraestructuras cognitivas auditables. Desde este contexto latinoamericano, GAME OVER propone una contribución abierta y reproducible al debate global sobre la regulación técnica de la inteligencia artificial, promoviendo un enfoque basado en transparencia, evidencia, responsabilidad institucional y control humano efectivo. En este sentido, el objetivo fundamental de GAME OVER no es sustituir el juicio humano ni restringir la innovación tecnológica. Su consiste en proporcionar las bases conceptuales, arquitectónicas y operativas que permitan el desarrollo de sistemas de inteligencia artificial capaces de actuar de forma responsable dentro de ecosistemas complejos propósito, garantizando que la automatización avanzada permanezca alineada con principios verificables de confianza, seguridad, trazabilidad y rendición de cuentas. En síntesis, este documento presenta una propuesta integral para la construcción de una nueva generación de infraestructuras digitales gobernadas, donde la inteligencia artificial deja de concebirse exclusivamente como una capacidad técnica y pasa a entenderse como una capacidad institucionalmente supervisada, explicable, verificable y responsable. documents.abstract: This study employs Systematic Literature and Network Analysis (SLNA) to explore game-based learning (GBL) in English language acquisition. A total of 1,774 publications on GBL and English as a Foreign Language (EFL), published between 2020 and 2025, were identified in Scopus, of which 444 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis. Citation network mapping and thematic clustering were conducted using VOSviewer to identify research trends and methodological developments. The findings reveal a growing emphasis on mobile technologies, artificial intelligence, immersive learning environments, and virtual reality applications in language learning, learner motivation, and vocabulary acquisition. Despite these advances, several limitations remain, including the lack of longitudinal studies examining long-term impacts, insufficient teacher training, and limited pedagogical integration of GBL practices. This study contributes to the existing literature by identifying emerging trends, gaps, and future research directions in the development and application of GBL in EFL contexts.

Background Coeliac disease diagnosis on duodenal biopsies is limited by interobserver variability. We have previously demonstrated pathologist-level performance with our artificial intelligence (AI) model for the histopathological diagnosis of adult coeliac disease, but not in paediatric practice. As paediatric coeliac disease screening programmes expand internationally, accurate and scalable diagnostic tools are needed. We investigated whether an AI model trained exclusively on adult whole-slide images (WSIs) can generalise to paediatric coeliac disease diagnosis across independent centres. Methods A training and validation dataset of 9958 WSIs from 8421 adult patients (961 coeliac disease; collected Jan 1, 2014, to March 31, 2025) from five centres was used to develop an ensemble of multiple-instance learning models using features from a foundation model. Testing was performed on 708 consecutive paediatric patients (86 with coeliac disease) from two centres (Edinburgh and Southampton) not included in training. Model calibration was assessed, and probability outputs were grouped into clinically interpretable categories. Findings In adult cross-validation, the AI model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 99.1% (95% CI 98.9–99.4), sensitivity of 89.3% (87.2–91.1), specificity of 98.8% (98.5–99.0), and negative predictive value (NPV) of 98.6% (98.3–98.9). On testing (paediatric) datasets, performance remained high (AUC 98.8%, 95% CI 98.2–99.4; sensitivity 80.2%, 70.6–87.3; specificity 98.4%, 97.1–99.1; NPV 97.3%, 95.7–98.3). Restricting analysis to predictions outside the intermediate-probability range (predicted coeliac disease probability <10% or ≥65%; 604 [85.3%] of 708 cases) improved sensitivity to 100% (95% CI 93.7–100.0) and specificity to 98.7% (97.4–99.4). No misclassifications were observed among high-confidence predictions (<2% or ≥85%; 467 [66.0%] of 708 cases). The expected calibration error was 0.03. Performance improved significantly when biopsies from both duodenal sites (bulb [D1] and descending [D2/3]) were considered. Interpretation Our AI model, trained on adult biopsies, generalises to paediatric coeliac disease diagnosis across centres and scanner platforms. Well calibrated probability outputs provide clinically interpretable measures of diagnostic confidence and could support safe identification of coeliac disease-negative biopsies within defined thresholds. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of applying adult-derived AI models in paediatric populations and reinforce the importance of multi-site (D1 & D2) biopsy sampling. Funding The National Institute for Health and Care Research.

documents.abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has prompted growing interest in its potential in intercultural competence (IC) education. Yet research on how GenAI can support IC development remains fragmented across language education, pragmatics, pedagogy, and professional communication. This scoping review mapped research contexts, designs, theoretical foundations, and findings on GenAI-mediated IC education. Eligible English-language publications published or posted between November 2022 and 11 August 2026 examined GenAI in relation to IC or related pragmatic and socio-pragmatic constructs of IC in higher education. Searches of ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar identified 26 eligible publications, including 20 empirical studies and 6 non-empirical publications. Data were charted using a structured form and synthesised descriptively and thematically. The included empirical studies reported varied perceived and task-specific outcomes for intercultural and pragmatic learning, mainly in structured and guided activities. Three issues warrant particular attention. First, the included publications drew on heterogeneous theoretical frameworks that addressed different or partial dimensions of IC. Second, several publications positioned teacher mediation as important for GenAI-supported learning, yet teacher preparedness, including their AI literacy and capacity to undertake this role, was not directly or systematically measured. Third, few studies directly examined learners’ critical AI literacy or the cognitive processes involved in evaluating or revising GenAI-generated content.

To address persistent issues in junior high chemistry teaching of Composition and Structure of Substances—including fragmented disciplinary perspectives, highly abstract micro-level concepts, and underdeveloped macro-submicro-symbolic triple representation thinking—this study constructs a four-stage interdisciplinary practical teaching model integrated with generative artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR). The teaching practice was implemented in a natural ninth-grade class (N=40) in Zhengzhou. To ensure in-depth analysis of the massive multimodal data generated by AI and VR interactions, purposive sampling was employed to select five representative students as a focus group. Following a single-group pretest-posttest design, data from this focus group were evaluated across four dimensions to systematically measure learning outcomes: macro cognition via concept maps, micro cognition via knowledge cards, model deepening through AI text error correction, and transfer competence and AI literacy via AI chat record coding. Post-intervention data revealed significant improvements across all dimensions. In macro cognition, average concept map nodes increased by 108.8% (from 6.8 to 14.2). For micro cognition, accuracy scores of micro-level tasks surged by 170.0% (from 1.0 to 2.7). Furthermore, the error correction rate reached 88.9% during model refinement, while critical probing questions accounted for 45.83% of total chat records, indicating enhanced transfer and AI literacy. These findings confirm that the generative AI-empowered interdisciplinary model effectively broadens students’ cognitive frameworks, lowers learning barriers of abstract chemical knowledge, consolidates mastery of model-based symbolic representation, and fosters preliminary AI critical literacy. It provides a practical, replicable reference for advancing digital interdisciplinary chemistry teaching at the junior high level.

This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

Purpose Firms are highly dependent on digitalization of their processes and procedures through the integration of generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI). Gen AI supports digital innovation (DI), which is crucial to innovation performance (IP). The purpose of this study is to examine how Gen AI capabilities, the knowledge creation process (KCP), and DI contribute to the creation of IP. Furthermore, the paper discusses the moderating effects of human and AI (AI-HI) collaboration, top management knowledge value (TMKV), and big data knowledge management (BDKM). Design/methodology/approach Data were collected via questionnaires from managers of Chinese manufacturing firms. PLS-SEM is used for hypothesis testing. Findings The findings indicated that Gen AI capabilities and KCP are significantly associated with DI. Similarly, DI influences innovation performance, and DI mediates the relationships among Gen AI capabilities, KCP, and IP. Furthermore, AI-HI collaboration moderates between Gen AI capabilities and DI. Similarly, TMKV moderates between KCP and DI. Lastly, BDKM moderates between DI and innovation performance. Practical implications The study provides actionable insights for managers and policymakers on the surge in Gen AI capabilities in decision-making. Originality/value Based on resource orchestration theory (ROT), this research paper examines how the orchestration of digital and knowledge resources enhances performance.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot into higher education has raised urgent questions about their effects on students' higher-order cognitive abilities. While these tools promise unprecedented access to information and cognitive support, growing concerns have emerged regarding the potential erosion of critical thinking skills among university students who adopt them uncritically. Despite increasing scholarly attention to artificial intelligence in education, systematic evidence on how generative AI relates to distinct dimensions of higher-order thinking remains limited. This systematic literature review, guided by the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline, aims to identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on the relationship between generative AI use and university students' analytical, evaluative, and creative thinking outcomes, using the higher-order cognitive processes of Bloom's Revised Taxonomy as an organizing framework. A comprehensive search across Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar yielded 847 initial records, of which 42 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria after screening. Thematic synthesis revealed heterogeneous outcomes: analytical thinking outcomes were generally positive under structured prompting conditions, evaluative thinking appeared most vulnerable in the absence of deliberate pedagogical design, and creative thinking outcomes were most frequently reported as positive. Across themes, the quality of pedagogical integration was the condition most frequently associated with favorable outcomes. This review contributes a dimension-level synthesis of generative AI and higher-order thinking, identifies the pedagogical conditions associated with favorable and unfavorable outcomes, and documents the heterogeneity of outcomes across studies, offering an evidence-informed framework for educators, curriculum designers, and policymakers seeking to use generative AI as a cognitive scaffold rather than a cognitive replacement.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Research on generative AI use in EMI nursing and health sciences contexts in the Gulf region remains limited. This study investigated the uses, experiences, and perceptions of generative AI among nursing and health science students at the Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET) in Kuwait. Using a single-institution convergent mixed methods survey design, quantitative and qualitative data were collected from 241 undergraduate students. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative responses were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that 94.6% of participants reported previous use of generative AI tools and 83.4% reported using them for academic purposes at least occasionally. Four interrelated themes emerged: (1) AI as a facilitator of English academic writing; (2) AI as a cognitive and academic efficiency tool; (3) AI as a confidence-building resource; and (4) students’ awareness of opportunities and risks associated with AI use. Students primarily used AI to improve grammar, vocabulary, idea generation, and writing organization. Participants also reported greater perceived confidence and reduced writing anxiety. Furthermore, participants expressed awareness of concerns regarding overreliance, inaccurate information, and academic integrity. The study contributes to emerging research on AI in higher education by highlighting students’ reported use and perceptions of AI in EMI health science contexts in Kuwait. The findings suggest the need for AI literacy frameworks that promote responsible and ethical use of AI in academic writing.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Precision pharmacology aims to select the most appropriate medicine, dose and monitoring strategy for an individual patient.Its translation is limited by fragmented records, incomplete biological characterization, timevarying physiology and the difficulty of converting high-dimensional evidence into a safe action.Generative health data science extends conventional prediction by learning structured representations of molecules, cells, patients and clinical trajectories and by producing reviewable candidates such as molecular structures, treatment options, synthetic records, counterfactual courses and dose scenarios.This critical review evaluates large language models, multimodal and biological foundation models, graph and diffusion architectures, syntheticpatient generators, digital twins and bounded agentic workflows across target discovery, repurposing, pharmacogenomics, treatment selection, individualised dosing and pharmacovigilance.Evidence is strongest for representation learning, structure-enabled discovery and selected pharmacogenomic pathways; autonomous patient-level treatment and dosing remain investigational.Recent advances include explainable drug-repurposing foundation models, multimodal clinical foundation models and a randomised phase 2a trial of a generative-AIdiscovered TNIK inhibitor.We propose a Data-to-Dose framework linking intended-use definition, data provenance, longitudinal patient-state modelling, constrained generation, mechanistic and causal checks, uncertainty-aware ranking, professional review and lifecycle monitoring.Generation must remain distinct from clinical authorisation, and synthetic-data fidelity must not be equated with privacy, fairness or external validity.Generative systems may become an enabling layer for precision pharmacology only when their creative capacity is bounded by pharmacology, evidence and accountable clinical judgment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This commentary examines gesture-based rehabilitation (GBR) as an assistive technology within an ecosystem for survivors of infectious diseases with neurological disabilities. It describes the roles of computer vision, markerless motion capture, depth cameras, artificial intelligence-driven pose estimation, wearable sensors, smartphone-based tracking, and virtual or augmented reality, while considering infection control and global accessibility. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This commentary was developed by synthesising the existing literature, with an emphasis on camera-based motion capture, gesture-controlled serious games, AI-driven pose estimation, wearable movement sensors, smartphone tracking, and virtual or augmented reality rehabilitation systems. The analysis compares outcomes from traditional neurological conditions, such as stroke and Parkinson's disease, to the specific needs of infectious disease survivors. RESULTS: Evidence from stroke, Parkinson's disease, and other neurological populations suggests that gesture-based systems may support motor rehabilitation, patient engagement, and remote monitoring. GBR may also reduce the need for direct patient-therapist interaction. However, there is currently insufficient direct evidence on the effectiveness, safety, and feasibility of these systems among survivors of infectious diseases. Additional barriers include hardware costs, limited digital infrastructure, and unequal access in rural and resource-constrained settings. CONCLUSION: GBR offers a versatile method for aiding recovery after infectious neurological illnesses. Nonetheless, its safety, effectiveness, and practicality in these groups remain uncertain, as most evidence comes from non-infectious neurological conditions. Specific studies on these populations are necessary before routinely recommending these technologies, along with strategies to overcome technological, financial, and access-related challenges.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is being investigated for renewable-energy forecasting, optimisation, predictive maintenance, synthetic-data generation, and infrastructure planning. This study reviews global advances and critically assesses their implications for Africa's sustainable energy transition. It aims to: (i) map GenAI applications in renewable-energy systems; (ii) distinguish demonstrated results from proposed African opportunities; (iii) evaluate evidence quality, transferability, and deployment feasibility; and (iv) identify context-specific research and policy priorities. A systematic review was reported using PRISMA 2020, with the PRALSMA AI-assisted workflow used to support, but not replace, researcher-led screening and synthesis. OpenAlex records published from 2020 to May 2026 were screened, yielding 75 included studies. Manual analysis was triangulated with ChatGPT Project and NotebookLM, and findings were weighted by methodological quality, evidence maturity, and relevance to African data, grid, infrastructure, institutional, and cost conditions. The corpus remains geographically imbalanced: five of the 75 included studies report an African institutional affiliation (Morocco, Nigeria, and South Africa, with further co-affiliations in Tunisia and Gabon), and most quantitative outcomes still derive from non-African simulations, prototypes, or case studies. Consequently, reported error, cost, emission, and accuracy improvements are treated as source-specific rather than directly transferable African effects. Near-term priorities are controlled pilots of lightweight, explainable, offline-capable decision support and synthetic-data methods; compute-intensive diffusion, agentic, digital-twin, and imitation-learning applications require further validation. GenAI may support African renewable-energy transitions, but benefits depend on local datasets, reliable fallback procedures, lifecycle environmental assessment, workforce capacity, governance, and staged field validation.

Abstract AI increasingly depends on globally distributed infrastructures, including advanced semiconductors, cloud platforms, data centres, foundation models, software frameworks and specialised labour. This dependence has intensified policy interest in AI sovereignty, which is often associated with domestic ownership of technological assets and the development of a nationally controlled AI stack. This article argues that ownership is neither a sufficient nor universally necessary condition of sovereign control. Instead, AI sovereignty should be understood as the capacity of public authorities to govern the dependencies through which critical AI capabilities are produced, accessed and sustained. The article develops the concept of functional AI sovereignty and identifies six interdependent dimensions of effective sovereign control: visibility, authority, allocation, substitutability, continuity and accountability. It then introduces sovereign orchestration as an institutional model through which governments can coordinate heterogeneous public and private AI resources using regulation, strategic procurement, interoperability, multi-provider routing, capacity clearing and selective public ownership. This model seeks to preserve access to private investment, international supply chains and distributed expertise while preventing individual providers from acquiring an irreversible veto over critical public functions. The article also specifies the limits of functional sovereignty. Orchestration requires sufficient public-sector expertise, access to operational information and credible technological alternatives. Direct ownership remains necessary where interruption costs are high, substitution is infeasible and external legal or geopolitical exposure is substantial. Effective AI sovereignty therefore lies not in eliminating technological interdependence, but in ensuring that critical dependencies remain visible, reversible, resilient and publicly accountable.

The increasing energy consumption of the Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) sector and the growing carbon emissions demonstrate the importance of sustainable software engineering practices. This study presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) covering the years 2020 to September 2025 to review and analyze research on green software metrics, tools, and validation methods. This study addresses five research questions, focusing on (i) green metrics, (ii) their place within the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), (iii) validation methodologies, (iv) measurement tools and models, and (v) the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The results obtained reveal that energy-focused metrics are widely discussed in the literature. Instruments and empirical experiments represent the most common methodological approaches used for validation. While emerging models demonstrate the place of machine learning in predictive energy forecasting, the use of AI remains limited, and standardized frameworks are lacking.

Primary Health Care (PHC) is the main gateway to the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), being responsible for health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and care coordination. In this context, this study aimed to develop a practical physiotherapy care guide to support physiotherapists working in PHC. This is a review based on documents from the Brazilian Ministry of Health and scientific evidence, addressing the main conditions managed at the primary care level, including low back pain, pneumonia, asthma, headache, epilepsy, repetitive strain injuries/work-related musculoskeletal disorders (RSI/WMSDs), and occupational health-related dysfunctions. The guide compiles assessment strategies, evidence-based physiotherapeutic interventions, referral criteria, and clinical flowcharts designed to support clinical decision-making. The findings highlight that physiotherapists enhance the effectiveness of PHC through individual and group interventions, home visits, health education, and participation in multidisciplinary teams. It is concluded that incorporating practical protocols and care strategies strengthens comprehensive care, promotes disease prevention, and contributes to improving functionality and quality of life among individuals receiving primary health care services.

The primary Indian technical textiles industry concern is to keep market responsiveness and attain operational efficiency, which will rank as a $22 billion business in 2024 ( Grand View Research, 2024 ). The study suggests the implementation of lean-agile enabled supply chain framework as part of the artificial intelligence that has been combined with hybrid lean-agile manufacturing to improve the competitive advantage of Indian technical textile-based manufacturing companies. This study conducted through theoretical synthesis of the Resource-Based View theory, Dynamic Capabilities framework, and supply chain innovation theory illustrates that a variety of AI technologies, such as machine learning, predictive analytics, and real-time optimization, enable lean efficiency targets as well as the agile responsiveness objectives to be met in parallel. The framework determines that there are four essential AI-enabled capabilities which include intelligent demand forecasting, adaptive inventory optimization, predictive quality management and dynamic supplier collaboration. According to synthesized research, organizations applying such AI-driven models demonstrate significant performance gains, including up to 87% forecasting accuracy , 93.45% defect detection rates , 65% faster disruption response times , and 24.9% reductions in aggregate inventory costs. The proposed model provides both theoretical advancement in understanding AI‘s role in supply chain strategy and practical implementation guidance for technical textile manufacturers seeking digital transformation.

documents.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to automate repetitive business processes, enhance employee capabilities and augment managerial decision-making across industries. However, many organisations struggle to translate AI initiatives into sustained strategic value. This gap between AI's potential and realised outcomes highlights the need to understand how organisations harness AI to generate business value, which this paper addresses. Design/methodology/approach We conducted a two-phase qualitative study of Transport and Logistics (T&L) organisations grounded in dynamic capabilities theory and its microfoundations. The first phase involved a systematic review of practitioner (grey) literature to examine AI applications, capabilities, processes and benefits across five T&L organisations. Phase 2 triangulated and refined these insights through key informant interviews. Findings The results indicate that T&L organisations adopt both generic AI technologies (e.g. chatbots, virtual assistants) and industry-specific AI-enabled systems (e.g. autonomous guided vehicles in warehouses, robotic forklifts and collaborative robots). When these AI assets are combined with specific microfoundations, such as AI skills, organisational routines and governance processes, they enable organisations to develop AI-based dynamic capabilities to sense, respond and transform transport, warehousing and delivery operations. These capabilities contribute to workers' safety, operational efficiency, customer experience and environmental sustainability. Originality/value The study contributes a model and propositions that explain how AI-based dynamic capabilities, underpinned by sociotechnical microfoundations enable organisations to gain operational and environmental advantages, offering guidance for managers embarking on an AI exploration journey.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Introduction: The minibus taxi industry underpins South Africa's public transport system, serving approximately 80.2% of daily commuters. Despite its economic importance, the sector operates in a high-stress, informal environment, exposing drivers to occupational health risks compounded by limited medical surveillance. This study explored healthcare-related challenges and barriers to healthcare access among taxi drivers, owners, and association representatives in the CoT. Methods: A participatory research design was used. Ninety-two participants (83 males, 9 females) were purposively sampled from taxi drivers, owners, and association representatives across CoT taxi ranks. Data were collected using eight focus group discussions, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using framework-informed, deductive thematic analysis. Results: Findings revealed layered systemic barriers: regulatory gaps, institutional distrust, and gendered stigma; geographic and infrastructural constraints, absent mental health services, and power imbalances between owners and drivers; conflicts between clinic hours and work schedules, rejection of medical certificates, and broken referral pathways; and deferred care, self-medication, and accumulated psychological strain. Conclusion: Taxi rank environments and rigid industry structures directly threaten drivers' physical and psychological well-being, fostering fatigue, substance use, and unresolved trauma. Interventions should prioritise decentralised, mobile healthcare aligned with operational hours and improved rank infrastructure to promote safer, dignified working conditions.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) path planning is widely applied in fields such as Internet of Things (IoT) environmental monitoring, intelligent transportation, low-altitude logistics, and autonomous inspection. With the rapid development of UAV intelligence, natural language task planning powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising research hotspot. However, in safety-critical flight missions, LLMs suffer from issues such as unstable structured outputs, insufficient understanding of complex constraints, and unreliable responses to dangerous inputs, which can jeopardize the safety and robustness of UAV path planning. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an LLM-based hierarchical safe and robust UAV path planning framework to achieve co-optimization of natural language task understanding and deterministic path search. We design a Prompt–RAG–Validator safety enhancement mechanism that improves the LLM’s safety decision-making capabilities through prompt constraints, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and rule validation, while constructing a structured constraint representation to convert natural language requirements into parsable planning constraints. Furthermore, we combine a grid cost map with the A* algorithm to achieve autonomous obstacle avoidance and safe grid-path generation. In addition, a two-stage evaluation system targeting both the constraint generation layer and the path-planning layer is constructed to verify model output reliability and actual planning performance. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed method across various complex scenarios, including multi-constraint tasks, risk-zone planning, incomplete input information, and prompt injection attacks. Notably, on the current template-derived benchmark, the deterministic regex/slot parser provided a stronger baseline with no dangerous outputs, whereas the LLM-based pipeline offers greater flexibility in handling diverse linguistic expressions.

Lee Gyoo Baek, Professor Emeritus, University of Ulsan (울산대학교 디자인건축융합학부 명예교수) This paper proposes Homo tokenatus, "the human equipped with tokens," as a concept for the human condition in an era when generative AI has become the basic infrastructure of everyday life. Large language models read the world in tokens and learn and speak by predicting the next token; the token is both the mode of being of AI and the unit by which its use is measured and priced. The paper structures the concept on three levels: technology (the nature of AI), economy (the unit of use), and humanity (the mode of life). It distinguishes the concept from Homo economicus, Phono sapiens, Homo silicus, and Homo Promptus, and discusses the problems of quantification, inequality, dependence, and value raised by a society in which human thought and labor are converted into tokens. The term Homo tokenatus is coined and first proposed by the author in this paper. 이 글은 생성형 AI가 일상의 기본 인프라가 된 시대의 인간을 '호모 토케나투스(Homo tokenatus)', 곧 '토큰을 갖춘 인간'으로 규정할 것을 제안한다. 대규모 언어모델(LLM)은 세계를 토큰 단위로 읽고 다음 토큰을 예측하는 방식으로 학습하고 말한다. 토큰은 AI의 존재 방식이자 AI 이용을 계량하고 값을 매기는 단위다. 이 글은 이 개념을 기술, 경제, 인간의 세 층위로 구조화하고 기존 개념과의 차이를 밝힌다. 호모 토케나투스는 필자가 이 글에서 처음 제시하는 개념이다.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human–AI collaboration supports manufacturing sustainability by minimizing time loss and resource waste, thereby enabling faster, more accurate decision-making. However, how AI transparency influences employee decision quality through cognitive appraisal remains underexplored, limiting guidance on balancing technological advancement with employee decision-making in manufacturing. Drawing on stress cognitive appraisal theory, this study examines the relationship between AI transparency and employee decision quality using structural equation modeling of questionnaire data from 321 intelligent manufacturing employees. Results show that AI transparency enhances employee decision quality by promoting challenge appraisal and reducing threat appraisal; both appraisals mediate this relationship. AI-enabled job complexity moderates the negative effect of AI transparency on threat appraisal and significantly moderates the mediating role of threat appraisal. However, its moderating effect on the relationship between AI transparency and challenge appraisal is nonsignificant. These findings provide practical guidance for developing and implementing human-centered AI systems in manufacturing to improve employee decision quality.
