documents.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is embedded in design education, yet little is known about how different tools reshape metacognition and the pathways linking ideas to outcomes. We compare three conditions, ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and a no-AI control, in a virtual reality cultural heritage serious game task with 51 novice designers. Think-aloud, screen recordings, sketches, and AI logs were coded into network-based cognitive maps and event-anchored indicators around metacognitive nodes. Analyses combine expert ratings of design outcomes with thinking pathway profiles and window diversity after metacognitive events. Both GenAI groups show higher mean design-quality ratings than the control, but in complementary ways. DeepSeek broadens early ideation and shows higher novelty ratings, while ChatGPT strengthens metacognitive regulation and structured convergence, aligning with higher systematicity and interactivity. The findings introduce process-sensitive indicators and phase-aware guidance for configuring exploration-oriented and regulation-oriented assistance in human and AI co-creation.

As information systems (IS) transition from deterministic rule-based engines to probabilistic machine learning architectures, the risk of systematic bias and disparate impact increases significantly. While advanced predictive models optimize across high-stakes domains—such as credit scoring, criminal justice, human resources, and biometric authentication, they frequently perpetuate historical inequities via proxy variables even when explicit sensitive attributes are omitted. This paper presents a detailed investigation into the theoretical foundations, mathematical formalisms, and systemic pipelines of "Fair AI." We propose an integrated sociotechnical framework spanning human perception, technological intervention, and organizational governance, fully incorporating recent advances in intelligent automation and secure architecture.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models for code have achieved strong performance across diverse software analytics tasks, yet their real-world adoption remains limited by high computational demands, slow inference speeds, significant energy consumption, and environmental impact. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical solution by transferring knowledge from a large model (teacher) to a smaller and more efficient model (student). Despite its effectiveness, recent studies show that models distilled from a single teacher often exhibit degraded adversarial robustness, even when robustness-aware distillation techniques are employed. These observations suggest a fundamental limitation of single-teacher distillation in simultaneously transferring high-quality and robust knowledge. To overcome this limitation, we propose Mixture of Experts Knowledge Distillation (MoEKD), a KD framework that leverages a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture to enable more effective and robust knowledge transfer from multiple specialized experts into a compact model. MoEKD decomposes the distillation process into expert and router training, aggregation of expert knowledge through a learned routing mechanism, and distillation from the aggregated knowledge. We evaluate MoEKD on the vulnerability detection task using CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT models. Experimental results show that MoEKD not only improves adversarial robustness by up to 35.8%, but also enhances predictive performance by up to 13%, compared to state-of-the-art KD baselines, including Compressor and AVATAR. Moreover, MoEKD-based students exhibit greater behavioral fidelity to their teachers, indicating better preservation of the teacher's predictive behavior after distillation. Deployment efficiency and environmental sustainability evaluations further show that MoEKD-based students maintain deployment costs comparable to their single-teacher counterparts, with slightly lower inference latency, energy consumption, and carbon emissions observed in most CPU and GPU settings. Our ablation analyses show that MoEKD retains its performance and robustness advantages under more aggressive student compression, while lightweight heterogeneous experts substantially reduce offline training costs and largely preserve its performance gains, but exhibit reduced adversarial robustness. The router analysis further shows that top-2 expert selection mitigates top-1 routing errors, while routing quality influences both the aggregated knowledge and the resulting student performance. Overall, these findings highlight the effectiveness of multi-expert knowledge aggregation in addressing key limitations of existing single-teacher KD approaches.

As large language models increasingly match human performance on moral-judgment tasks, two bodies of literature have developed in parallel. Empirical moral psychology treats moral judgment as an output and benchmarks artificial systems against human responses. The philosophy of artificial moral agency denies agency to such systems mainly on the ground of sentience, an empirically inaccessible criterion that has left the debate stalled. This paper argues that human–AI convergence in moral judgment conceals a categorical asymmetry that neither literature has theorized. Drawing on Spinoza’s conatus and Damasio’s account of homeostasis and affect, it argues that moral agency presupposes affective-homeostatic self-maintenance as its constitutive ground: the organization from which valuation first arises. This condition is necessary but not sufficient, and the claim is constitutive rather than normative, so it does not derive an “ought” from an “is.” Sentience is repositioned as the experiential manifestation of this organization rather than the explanatory terminus. Contemporary AI systems, including those trained with human feedback, are therefore moral judges without moral agency. The paper closes with a behavioral research program, including concrete experimental designs, on the conditions under which people attribute moral agency to human and artificial agents.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: BART (Bay Area Rapid Transit) serves commuters, students, and visitors in the Bay Area. However, ridership has declined due to rising crimes, drug use, sexual assaults, and homelessness. These challenges disproportionately impact women and minorities, many of whom report discomfort, distrust in the system, and negative safety perceptions (Alliance for Girls Youth, 2024). The goal is to examine how safety perception influences BART riders’ experiences and decision making through the lenses of Human Factors and Industrial Engineering. We conducted a mixed-method research to understand perceived risk, environmental awareness, and support riders’ needs when commuting. Participants, particularly women, had reported feeling unsafe at night, traveling in groups, strategically choosing seatings, and staying vigilant in fear of being harmed. Riders also expressed interest in a verified “buddy feature,” safety alerts, and reporting incidents. Overall, this highlights opportunities to improve safety, build trust, and improve the commuting experience for BART.

This study examined how project managers navigate wicked problem dynamics in project environments with ambiguous problem definitions, contested stakeholder interests, evolving constraints, and no definitive solutions. Drawing on eight nested discussion sessions comprising 24 small-group conversations with 168 experienced project professionals across diverse industries, supplemented by 12 follow-up interviews, the study used a theory-informed abductive qualitative design. Adaptive leadership and wicked problem concepts informed the discussion prompts, whereas initial coding remained open to participants’ accounts rather than applying a predetermined adaptive-leadership coding framework. We then iteratively interpreted emergent patterns using wicked problems theory, adaptive leadership, and sensemaking as sensitizing theoretical lenses. The analysis identified five recurring adaptive practices: diagnostic framing, collaborative sensemaking, situational awareness, emotional regulation, and transparent communication. These practices illuminate how project managers develop workable problem definitions, engage competing perspectives, and coordinate action when technical expertise and established plans are insufficient. The study provides an empirically grounded account of leadership practice in temporary organizations and identifies practice-oriented implications for responding to wicked problem dynamics within time-bounded project settings.

Near-real-time wildfire monitoring is essential for situational awareness and emergency response. The Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) observes at 2 km every 5 min, whereas the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) observes at 375 m twice daily, leaving neither sensor able to track rapidly evolving fires in fine spatial detail. This study introduces a two-step deep learning approach that statistically infers VIIRS-like sub-pixel fire segmentation and brightness temperature (BT) from GOES imagery. The dataset comprises 257 U.S. wildfires within preselected regions of interest, pairing multi-spectral GOES imagery with VIIRS-derived references in four classes (Non-Fire, Small, Medium, and Large) defined by the number of fire pixels. Against an autoencoder-based baseline, the proposed method raises average precision from 0.105 to 0.368 and reduces the fire region BT root mean square error by 72.1% from 81.33 K to 22.69 K. Omission error rates fall from 9.41% to 1.96% for Medium fires and remain at zero for Large fires, whereas Small fires, 37% of the test set, remain at 39.91%. The false positive rate on Non-Fire images falls from 66.86% to 8.48%, near the operational GOES product’s 6.36% with lower omission (31.40% versus 40.35%). Inference completes within 5 min of observation for a monitored region.

The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has disrupted the invisible normative infrastructure of universities at multiple points simultaneously. Unlike previous technological transitions, AI enters the higher education system concurrently through three interconnected levels: the student level, where the meaning of assignments, exams, and individual work is renegotiated; the faculty level, where authorship, peer review, course preparation, and assessment practices are reshaped; and the institutional level, where academic integrity policies, accreditation processes, and relations of trust with publishers are restructured. This simultaneous and systemic disruption produces a relational normative phenomenon that individualistic accounts of AI usage fail to adequately capture. This chapter develops a conceptual framework by bringing together social norm theory in the tradition of Bicchieri and Coleman, the structural social network analysis of Granovetter, Burt, Valente, and Centola, and the sociology of higher education following Bourdieu and Bernstein. It identifies five sets of norms undergoing simultaneous transformation (authorship and ownership of work, assessment and its meaning, pedagogical authority, knowledge ownership, and academic productivity expectations) and analyzes how four properties of academic networks (density, brokerage, centrality, and boundary permeability) shape the speed, direction, and stability of normative change. The primary contribution is a systemic reading that traces AI-induced norm flows vertically across student, faculty, and institutional levels. Here, AI is read not as a novel tool but as a relational actor circulating within academic networks, accelerating certain norms, eroding others, and triggering the emergence of new normative consensuses.

documents.abstract: In 1985, Richard Stallman introduced copyleft, a licensing principle that allows source code to be used, modified, and redistributed provided that the same freedoms are preserved in derivative works (Stallman, 1985). Although developed for software, copyleft offers a useful analogy for ecological research, where data, metadata, and analytical code should be accessible and reusable under clear licenses. Similarly, our ability to understand and address ecological challenges such as biodiversity loss, species range shifts, land degradation, and climate change depends on ecological knowledge being open where ethically appropriate and otherwise responsibly accessible. Such knowledge should also be managed according to the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) and established domain standards such as Darwin Core and Ecological Metadata Language (Wieczorek et al. 2012, Wilkinson et al. 2016). Despite substantial progress in open science (Dwivedi et al. 2022), many key ecological datasets (e.g., national ecological inventories, biodiversity records, and high-spatial- and temporal-resolution remote-sensing data) remain proprietary or available only with restricted access (e.g., requiring formal approval). These gaps are substantial: Large-scale analyses of hundreds of millions of ecological records reveal persistent taxonomic, geographic, and temporal biases (Meyer et al. 2015, Daru and Rodriguez, 2023). Much of the scientific literature also remains behind paywalls, while open-access publication fees can create barriers for researchers with limited funding (Rocchini and Neteler 2012). This paradox, that is, publicly funded knowledge becoming inaccessible to the public, constrains who can participate in ecological research and which ecosystems, regions, and perspectives are ultimately represented. AI does not create this problem but can amplify it by embedding data biases in models reused at scale, while closed training data limit independent scrutiny (Koch et al. 2022). AI for ecology encompasses task-specific machine-learning and computer-vision models, as well as foundation models, including large language models (LLMs). These systems differ in scale, purpose, and accessibility, but all depend on the quality, documentation, and governance of the data used to train and evaluate them. By integrating diverse data sources, AI can transform ecological research. However, when data, code, or model-development processes cannot be independently inspected, existing knowledge gaps and biases may be transferred into ecological inference. Appropriately open, reliable, and interoperable ecological data, together with transparent and auditable AI infrastructures, are therefore essential for robust, equitable, and epistemically sound ecological research. The expansion of AI in ecological research intensifies the need for transparent and well-documented knowledge. Bias is not unique to AI: statistical, mechanistic, and machine-learning models can all inherit limitations from their data and assumptions. AI can increase the scale, opacity, and reach of these effects (Han et al. 2023). Currently, many applications in ecology use task-specific AI models trained for bounded prediction or classification problems (Pichler and Hartig 2023). These models are often trained on specialized aggregated ecological repositories (e.g., biodiversity data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility [GBIF]), climatic variables (e.g., from WorldClim and ERA5), or land-use and land cover change mapping (e.g., from satellite imagery). In contrast, the rise of foundation models, including LLMs used for the automated synthesis of scientific literature, code generation, data processing and analysis, requires massive cross-domain training sets that are difficult to build from scratch. Consequently, models trained on skewed, geographically biased, or inaccessible datasets can systematically misrepresent under-sampled regions and reflect long-standing inequities in ecological knowledge. When training datasets are inaccessible, their composition is also difficult to inspect, making gaps in the representation of regions, languages, taxa, or perspectives harder to detect and evaluate. Thus, LLMs are not necessarily more biased than task-specific AI models, but their biases can be harder to trace and hence propagate across a wider range of users, tasks, and applications. In ecology, both task-specific and generic models inherit the limitations of the data used to train them. For example, species-recognition models inherit taxonomic imbalances in training images (Koch et al. 2022), whereas LLMs can process ecological information rapidly but may perform poorly on specific tasks. Gougherty and Clipp (2024) found that LLMs often struggled to extract pathogen-incidence values and sometimes inferred that all individuals were affected when no incidence value was reported. Similarly, Dorm et al. (2026) showed that LLMs performed poorly in generating species range maps and offered only limited improvement over random guessing in threat classification. Comparable effects have been observed in other AI domains, where imbalances in training data have produced systematically poorer model performance for underrepresented groups (Birhane, 2022). Together, these examples illustrate how unbalanced training data can transfer existing knowledge gaps into model outputs, highlighting the importance of identifying, documenting, and reducing such biases before models are applied beyond their validated domain. AI models can furthermore introduce subtler epistemic risks (Loru et al. 2025), including the confident fabrication of ecological information, the misrepresentation of species-trait responses to environmental gradients, and the generation of unsupported ecological interactions or spatial patterns. In ecological applications, documented limitations already include errors in quantitative information extraction and uneven performance across tasks (Gougherty and Clipp, 2024, Dorm et al. 2026). For these reasons, responsible openness and transparent governance of ecological data and metadata are vital, because the reliability of specialized models and large-scale synthesis depends on whether foundational ecological resources can be appropriately accessed, documented, and independently evaluated. Reproducible evaluation therefore requires practical commitments. Ecological AI studies should provide standardized documentation describing where their training data came from, which taxa, regions, and environmental conditions they cover, how the model is intended to be used, and its known limitations. Established tools such as datasheets for datasets and model cards can support this documentation (Gebru et al. 2021). Models should also be evaluated across taxa, regions, languages, and environmental conditions, and data, code, prompts, model weights, and independent evaluation sets should be released where ethically, legally, and technically possible (Maasri et al. 2022, Smith et al. 2024). In order to improve data exchange and utilization, general principles and standards for the creation, verification, and sharing of data should be established while respecting the owners and creators of specific databases. Any restrictions and access procedures should also be documented. Public initiatives such as the Minerva LLM (Orlando et al. 2024) illustrate the value of transparent, language-specific model development, but openness alone does not ensure ecological or cultural validity across regions. AI also changes the politics of openness by creating a risk that openly shared data and open-source code are incorporated into proprietary models without reciprocal access, attribution, credit, or participation for the researchers, developers, and communities who produced them. In public and public/private programs such as GenAI4EU (2025), adequate funding should mean sustained support for data curation, digitization of legacy records, targeted collection in documented gaps, local skills and infrastructure, and independent auditing, not only model development. Funders, publishers, scientific societies, and research institutions should recognize data curation as a research output and require transparent documentation and evaluation. Collaboration should connect local communities and data holders to national infrastructures, international repositories, and standards bodies. Identifying and reducing bias in AI development, enabling robust validation, and sustaining open infrastructures all depend fundamentally on the availability of high-quality, representative, and well-documented ecological data. Where data are scarce, uneven, or unreliable, transparency becomes especially important for identifying gaps and assessing their consequences (Titley et al. 2017). Open data and governance policies must therefore be accompanied by dedicated funding for targeted data collection, the digitization of legacy records, curation, metadata preparation, quality control, local computational infrastructure, training, and equitable collaboration, particularly in under-sampled regions. Such investments are necessary to prevent openness from disproportionately benefiting institutions that already possess the resources needed to exploit shared datasets. Openness should not, however, imply unrestricted public release. Precise locations of threatened species, Indigenous and local knowledge, and data governed by consent or legal agreements may require spatial generalization, controlled access, embargoes, or community authority (Tulloch et al. 2018). Data should instead be as open as possible and as protected as necessary, combining FAIR data stewardship with the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics) where Indigenous or community-governed data are involved. International coordination among funders, ecological societies, repositories, publishers, data providers, and model developers is also needed to establish interoperable standards for data collection, annotation, documentation, sharing, and controlled access. Differences in the quality, resolution, and accessibility of ecological datasets should be explicitly documented and considered during model development and evaluation rather than remaining hidden (Dwivedi et al. 2022). Without shared standards and a commitment to responsible openness, ecological AI risks becoming fragmented, opaque, and shaped primarily by actors with the greatest computational and data resources. The practical priorities that we highlight are the following. Ecologists, AI researchers, funders, journals, repositories, and ecological societies should: audit geographic, taxonomic, temporal, and, where relevant, linguistic gaps in AI training and evaluation data, and quantify their effects on model performance; fund targeted data collection and the digitization of legacy records where these gaps have meaningful consequences; require machine-readable metadata and licenses, provenance records, uncertainty documentation, datasheets for datasets, and model cards; maintain independent benchmark datasets stratified across regions, taxa, sensors, and environmental conditions; and ensure that data-producing communities have access to computational infrastructure, training, credit, and decision-making roles rather than being treated solely as data providers (Wilkinson et al. 2016, Smith et al. 2024). Ecological research stands at a decisive crossroad: As AI reshapes how we observe and interpret the natural world, the openness and responsible governance of our data, models, and publications will determine whether this transformation is equitable and scientifically robust. Unrepresentative datasets, or data and models that cannot be independently evaluated, risk narrowing ecological insight, reinforcing global disparities, and introducing epistemic distortions that degrade our collective understanding of ecological systems. A well-governed, participatory, and inclusive ecological knowledge system, open where possible and protected where necessary, supported by public LLM research, auditable domain-specific models, and genuinely accessible publishing practices, is crucial to ensure that AI becomes a tool for discovery and justice rather than distortion. Just as copyleft preserved the freedoms to use, modify, and share software, responsible openness can free environmental science from informational silos while respecting legitimate restrictions. In the age of AI, openness is not only a technical requirement but an ethical obligation: Shared and responsibly governed knowledge is the foundation of collective solutions. There are no new data associated with this article. The authors declare no competing interests.

Abstract Evaluation and assessment research in health communication requires structured, construct-based approaches for interpreting visual materials. This study introduces the Asclepius Biological Interpretability Scale, developed through a two-stage modified Delphi process (a joint image-and-item panel followed by an independent item-only panel) grounded in the Biopsychosocial Model and Visual Literacy Theory, and examines whether multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems can reproducibly apply this framework relative to internally generated human reference scores. Six artworks (four health-themed and two controls) were evaluated by three multimodal AI models and four researchers (internal human reference) using a standardized protocol with independent researcher-operated accounts, memory-isolation procedures, repeated assessments over two days, and the final 20-item scale. Because Image Type varied across only six stimuli, health-themed versus control differences were summarized at the image level (Cohen’s d), human–AI differences were summarized descriptively at the rater level, and reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Spearman correlations. Within this development image set, AI-generated scores were descriptively higher for health-themed than for control images on the three biomedical subscales (image-level Cohen’s d = 0.91–1.38) but not on Non-Medical Interpretability (d = 0.49); with four health-themed and two control images, these differences were not statistically significant ( p = 0.19–0.60). Reproducibility across researcher-operated accounts was excellent for the three biomedical subscales (ICC = 0.90–0.97) and moderate for Non-Medical Interpretability (ICC = 0.57), whereas agreement across assessment days was poor (ICC = 0.04–0.46). The four researchers’ internal reference scores were higher than the AI-generated scores on the biomedical subscales for health-themed images (mean differences 1.41–1.96 points) and lower on Non-Medical Interpretability (− 2.02 to − 2.19 points). These findings provide preliminary methodological evidence that multimodal AI can reproducibly apply a structured interpretability framework to controlled visual stimuli. Although day-to-day stability and the Non-Medical Interpretability subscale, which showed substantial internal-consistency problems, require further refinement, the results support the feasibility of using AI as standardized non-human raters within controlled methodological settings. Broader validation using authentic health communication materials and independent external human raters remains necessary.

documents.abstract: Abstract The automotive industry’s operations face a critical dilemma: achieving high productivity while maintaining adequate ergonomic standards. High-volume production amplifies this condition, because the frequency of task execution keeps ergonomic risk ever-present. This work presents a real case from an automotive body parts assembly line. The objectives are to minimize the maximum individual ergonomic risk throughout job-rotation periods along a daily journey, and to optimize productivity by determining the optimal worker-to-workstation assignments. The Occupational Repetitive Action (OCRA) index is used to assess the risk of upper extremity musculoskeletal disorders. To solve this bi-objective problem, two algorithms are proposed: an $$\varepsilon $$ ε -constraint approach and a Tchebychev method. Both are grounded in a novel Integer Linear Programming (ILP) model tailored to integrate ergonomic and productivity considerations. The algorithms generated a complete Pareto front of 16 efficient solutions within a reasonable computational time. Managerial insights are derived, highlighting the inherent trade-off between the makespan and ergonomic risk, providing valuable guidelines for balancing worker well-being and productivity in assembly-line operations.

This study analyzes the relationship between digitalization, structural transformation, and carbon emission intensity in six ASEAN countries, namely Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, and Cambodia. The study uses annual panel data for the period 2004–2024, with the main estimation period covering 2010–2024. Carbon emission intensity is used as the dependent variable, while the number of internet users, industry value added, urban population, GDP per capita, international trade, and services sector value added are used as independent variables. All variables are transformed into natural logarithms so that the coefficients can be interpreted as elasticities. Estimation is conducted using the Fixed Effects Model with period fixed effects and Panel EGLS with period weights following model selection tests. The results show that digitalization, proxied by the number of internet users, has a positive but statistically insignificant relationship with carbon emission intensity. In contrast, industry value added, urban population, GDP per capita, and international trade have positive and significant relationships. Services sector value added has a negative and significant relationship with carbon emission intensity. These findings indicate that structural transformation toward the services sector is associated with lower emission intensity, while industrial expansion, urbanization, economic growth, and trade are associated with increased carbon emission intensity in the countries examined.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) for learning in higher education supports information retrieval, understanding of learning materials, reference searches, and the completion of academic assignments. However, its use raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty, responsibility, critical thinking skills, and potential dependence on technology. This study aimed to describe Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) students’ perceptions of the ethics of AI use in learning at UIN Sjech M. Djamil Djambek Bukittinggi. The study employed a descriptive qualitative approach involving three PAI students as primary informants and two lecturers as supporting informants, selected based on their relevance to the research focus. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, then analyzed using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s model through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings showed that students viewed AI as a tool that made learning easier, with its use requiring information verification, an understanding of sources, and critical thinking. AI use considered ethical included refraining from copying answers directly, conducting independent analysis, and maintaining AI’s role as a support for the thinking process. These findings underscore the importance of AI literacy, academic integrity, and students’ responsibility in PAI learning. This study provides a contextual account of students’ ethical perceptions and offers input for students, lecturers, and the study program to develop critical and responsible use of AI.

documents.abstract: This article examines the linguodidactic foundations for forming and developing the AI competence of both educators and students within the context of the effective use of artificial intelligence technologies in language education. Amidst digital transformation, artificial intelligence-specifically generative language models, chatbots, speech recognition systems, automated assessment tools, and adaptive learning platforms-is becoming a new component of the foreign language teaching and learning process. The article defines an educator's AI competence as a composite of technological knowledge, methodological-pedagogical competence, critical evaluation skills, awareness of ethics and digital security, and the ability to integrate AI tools into language education.

Kelawi Tourism Village, South Lampung, has strong community-based tourism potential, but the Minang Rua Bahari Tourism Awareness Group (Pokdarwis) faces communication barriers when serving international visitors. This Community Service Program (PKM) aimed to strengthen Pokdarwis capacity through an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted voice service as a communication support tool. The program was conducted from 12 to 14 June 2026 and involved 15 Pokdarwis members. Activities included problem identification, local knowledge development and validation, QR-based service implementation, training, mentoring, and evaluation at four service points: visitor reception, turtle conservation, Green Canyon, and homestay and culinary services. Results showed an increase in partner capacity from 58.2% in the pre-test to 91.8% in the post-test, representing a 33.6 percentage-point improvement. Participant satisfaction reached 92%, while partner and visitor achievement rates reached 95.2% and 94.5%, respectively. The program demonstrates that AI can support communication, conservation, safety, and the delivery of local cultural and culinary information without replacing the role of Pokdarwis.

The study assessed the perceptions of academic staff on the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital connectivity for transformative educational management in tertiary institutions in Bayelsa State. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, guided by two research questions. The population comprised academic staff from selected public universities and colleges of education in Bayelsa State, from which a sample of 350 respondents was drawn using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence and Digital Connectivity in Educational Management Questionnaire (AIDEMQ), validated by experts and yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.89 via Cronbach's alpha. Descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) were used to answer the research questions. The findings revealed that academic staff generally perceived AI as enhancing administrative efficiency through improved decision-making, error reduction, transparency, and time management, although challenges such as inadequate training and limited practical application constrained its full potential. Similarly, digital connectivity was perceived as effective in improving communication, collaboration, information dissemination, and the quality of teaching and learning, though gaps in infrastructure and system functionality limited its impact on administrative planning and scheduling. The study concluded that while AI and digital connectivity hold significant potential for transforming educational management, targeted interventions including capacity building, infrastructure enhancement, and strategic system integration are necessary to fully realize these benefits. Recommendations included providing regular staff training, investing in robust digital infrastructure, and implementing supportive policies to optimize the integration of AI and digital tools in tertiary institutions.

Abstract Agentic AI systems commonly combine a general-purpose AI model with prompts, tools, orchestration and an external memory layer. The model need not be fine-tuned: records retrieved from persistent memory are normally inserted into the model’s inference-time context and can thereby influence later outputs and actions without changing model weights. This article asks how far the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2) already govern the risks that follow. It reframes persistent memory as a system feature that can mediate or amplify misalignment and emergent behaviour, rather than as training data or a new category in the AI Act’s use-case-based taxonomy. Article 15 provides a clear legal anchor for robustness and cybersecurity, while Articles 9–14, 25, 72 and 73 extend coverage across risk management, data governance, logging, oversight, value-chain responsibility and post-market monitoring. For organisations within NIS2’s scope, Articles 20, 21 and 23 add entity-level governance, all-hazards cybersecurity, supply-chain controls and incident reporting. The remaining problem is therefore not a wholesale absence of law. It is whether these overlapping duties are sufficiently operationalised for memory-mediated failures such as poisoned retrieval, scope leakage, stale reliance, revocation failure and loss of provenance. The article proposes proportionate implementation through existing guidance, standards, documentation and monitoring mechanisms, without creating a new statutory risk tier or a memory-specific regulatory regime.

documents.abstract: Background and objective: Integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare and medical research represents significant potential; however, it also introduces practical and ethical challenges. This study analyzes physicians' perceptions of AI implementation in clinical and academic settings, exploring their awareness, perceptions, barriers, concerns, and insights into ethical and regulatory considerations. Methods: A mixed-methods approach was used. The quantitative component involved standardized surveys completed by 390 physicians (241 clinical, 149 academic) in Erbil City from November 2024 to June 2025. Participants were selected using systematic sampling, and surveys were self-administered. The qualitative component included two focus group discussions, involving 6 clinical physicians and 8 academic physicians, to explore in-depth perceptions and concerns regarding AI in healthcare and research. Results: Of 390 physicians, the majority of participants were male (69.2%). Mean age was 46.7±7 years. Familiarity with AI was higher among younger, male, and academic physicians, with age showing a negative association (p <0.001). Clinical physicians reported more concerns regarding privacy in healthcare (p=0.003) and research (p=0.041), as well as algorithmic bias (p=0.030). Despite these concerns, most physicians valued AI in healthcare and academic research and demonstrated strong interest in training and collaboration. Qualitative findings showed optimism and frequent use of AI tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek, often described as “Google replacements.” However, physicians also highlighted ethical issues and the need for local training and infrastructure improvement. Conclusion: Physicians generally welcome the use of AI in healthcare and research but emphasize the necessity of ethical guidelines, peer collaboration, and formal education. To ensure responsible adoption, addressing infrastructural and trust barriers will be essential for guaranteeing that AI technologies improve rather than undermine patient care and research integrity.

documents.abstract: Classical Forrestal penetration calculations are attractive because they are explicit, but their empirical strength-only resistance term is too restrictive for heterogeneous concrete-penetration data. This study derives a closed-form resistance equation from a governed literature dataset, reducing 497 raw records from 41 source blocks to 443 useable records from 37 sources through duplicate removal, governed density completion, deep-penetration filtering, and descriptor-only anomaly screening. Forrestal inversion maps each measured penetration depth to an operator-consistent effective resistance target described by mechanics-informed dimensionless descriptors. The artificial-intelligence contribution is a constrained equation-discovery workflow in which a categorical gradient-boosting model learns the nonlinear resistance surface, Shapley additive explanations restrict the analytical term family, and limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno optimization with bound constraints identifies equation coefficients under a forward penetration-depth objective. The engineering contribution is a 16-term explicit resistance law that replaces the empirical resistance relation inside the Forrestal operator while retaining its deterministic calculation form. On the 89-record held-out set, the equation gives a coefficient of determination of 0.9543 and a mean absolute percentage error of 14.88%, compared with 0.9206 and 24.44% for classical Forrestal and 0.9551 and 13.95% for the nonlinear resistance-reference model; its mean prediction-to-measurement ratio is 0.984. Repeated random, source-grouped, strength-stratified, out-of-distribution, input-uncertainty, and density-robustness tests bound the useable domain. The 80–120 MPa interval remains cautionary because of weaker held-out accuracy and limited cross-source support.

This conceptual working paper examines how Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NHR) can serve as a rigorous framework for political critique and accountability. Its normative criterion is the preservation and flourishing of human life, assessed through six equally ranked basic needs: thinking, health, security, social belonging, self-realization and participation, and meaning. Drawing on three complementary theoretical prompts, the paper addresses diplomatic and personal rapprochement with Vladimir Putin, the proposed livestreaming of an execution in the United States, and insufficient climate action. It distinguishes documented events, normative judgments and explanatory hypotheses. What is new in this article is the explicit formulation of the NHR’s political firmness: personal loyalty, public displays of authority and short-term interests must be assessed against their consequences for affected people. The paper translates this principle into a practical procedure involving evidence, participation, public justification and correction of harmful decisions. Within the series, the article connects the anthropological and systemic foundations of the NHR with concrete political evaluation. It extends the discussion of the right to think, human-AI collaboration and ecological responsibility toward institutional accountability. Prepared by Jean-Pol Martin in collaboration with ChatGPT. The paper includes an abstract, theoretical foundations, three illustrative applications, an accountability procedure and references. Current-event evidence is dated to 12 October 2026.

Abstract This paper examines theoretical aspects of human-AI communication, arguing that current AI systems, or ‘pragmatics-zombies,’ can mimic human-like pragmatic competence without genuine understanding. While these systems are increasingly adept at natural language interaction, their lack of subjective experience, intentionality, and embodied cognition creates a fundamental trust deficit, particularly in high-stakes scenarios. We argue that forcing human-to-human pragmatic frameworks onto these non-human entities is suboptimal, leading to issues in efficiency, robustness, and transparency. To address this, we introduce the concept of ‘Abstract Pragmatics,’ a general framework that allows for multiple, distinct pragmatic systems. We propose that instead of pursuing flawless mimicry of human communication, research should focus on developing novel, alternative pragmatic systems specifically designed for human-AI interaction. This approach would prioritize clarity, verifiability, and trustworthiness, fostering a more effective and reliable collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence by acknowledging and adapting to the unique nature of the machine.

Background: Cancer survivors of reproductive age face substantial risks of treatment-induced gonadotoxicity, yet clinical decision-making for fertility preservation remains largely empirical and population-based.A precision oncofertility framework that integrates genomic, biomarker, and toxicity data is urgently needed.Objective: To develop and validate a multimodal foundation model that integrates genomic variants, sex-specific reproductive biomarkers, treatment toxicity profiles, and clinical variables to predict fertility impairment risk and support individualized fertility-preservation decisions in cancer patients.Methods: A retrospective observational cohort of 400 patients (age 18-45 years) diagnosed with breast cancer, lymphoma, leukemia, testicular cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, or colorectal cancer was assembled.All patients received fertility-preservation counselling prior to treatment.Data included reproductive biomarkers (anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), antral follicle count (AFC), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), estradiol; sperm concentration, motility, testosterone, inhibin-B), genomic features (BRCA1, BRCA2, CHEK2, TP53, FMR1), treatment toxicity variables (alkylating agent and platinum exposure, radiation dose, stem cell transplantation), and standard clinical covariates.A transformer-based foundation model with four specialised encoders and cross-modal attention was developed.Performance was benchmarked against Random Forest, XGBoost, and a Deep Neural Network using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC).Results: The foundation model achieved the highest performance across all metrics: accuracy 0.883, precision 0.876, recall 0.862, F1 0.869, and AUC 0.934.AMH (importance score 0.187), AFC (0.171), and alkylating agent exposure (0.152) were the strongest predictors.Fertility risk stratification identified 37.0% (n=148) low-risk, 35.5% (n=142) moderate-risk, and 27.5% (n=110) high-risk patients.BRCA1/2 mutations and radiation dose independently amplified impairment risk.Conclusion: A precision oncofertility framework incorporating multimodal data and transformer-based architecture substantially outperforms conventional machine-learning approaches.AI-guided risk stratification can enable individualized, evidence-based fertility-preservation counselling and intervention, with direct implications for clinical oncofertility practice.

Preparing engineers for rapidly changing sociotechnical environments requires a clear account of the competencies that undergraduate engineering programs should foster. This study used the term future outstanding engineers to refer to engineering undergraduates being prepared for engineering excellence and examined the structure and correlates of their self-reported core competence. Cross-sectional survey data were obtained from 578 engineering undergraduates at a Chinese research university. A reflective–formative higher-order model was estimated using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM); partial least squares multigroup analysis (PLS-MGA) compared grade cohorts; and multiple linear regression examined associations with student background and educational experience. Adaptive, professional, and basic competence formed the higher-order construct, with adaptive competence receiving the largest outer weight. The outer weight of adaptive competence was larger, and that of professional competence smaller, among third-year than first-year students; the outer weight of basic competence did not differ significantly. Selected co-curricular and language-learning experiences were associated with adaptive competence, whereas family background and leadership experience were associated with professional competence. Basic competence was associated with a broader set of student background and engagement variables. These findings support a differentiated, stage-sensitive approach to competence development. Because the data are cross-sectional, self-reported, and drawn from one institution, the results should be interpreted as structural and associational rather than developmental or causal.

This PLC Laboratory Manual is an educational and practical resource designed to support undergraduate learning in Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and industrial automation. The material combines fundamental theoretical concepts with laboratory-oriented procedures to help students understand PLC architecture, programming principles, input/output systems, control logic, and practical automation applications.The manual introduces students to PLC hardware and software environments and provides structured laboratory activities that emphasize practical implementation, testing, simulation, monitoring, and troubleshooting. It also supports the development of essential skills in ladder logic programming, digital and analog I/O handling, control sequencing, timers and counters, and the integration of PLCs with industrial devices and automation systems.Each laboratory activity is organized to connect theoretical concepts with hands-on engineering practice, enabling students to gradually develop the ability to design, implement, test, and evaluate PLC-based control solutions. The material is intended to strengthen students’ understanding of industrial control systems while promoting problem-solving, logical thinking, and practical automation skills.This resource is suitable for undergraduate students, instructors, and learners in Automation, Artificial Intelligence, Systems Engineering, Control Engineering, Mechatronics, and related engineering disciplines who are interested in gaining practical experience with PLC-based industrial automation.The laboratory material can be used as a teaching resource for university laboratory sessions, practical training, and introductory study of programmable control systems and modern industrial automation.

The lack of well-fitting and supportive sports bras is a significant public health barrier, hindering adolescent girls from engaging in physical activity and negatively impacting their physical and mental health. This study aims to optimize sports bra design through seamless construction to improve aesthetics, comfort, support, and user satisfaction. A comparative analysis between proposed seamless designs and conventional sports bras evaluated anthropometric fit, biomechanical pressure distribution, and subjective user feedback. The proposed seamless design outperformed the conventional bras in both objective and subjective measures. It received high subjective ratings for support and satisfaction and provided favourable breast shaping. All measured pressures were within a comfortable threshold (<0.96 kPa), and arm movement significantly influenced breast morphology, underscoring the need for dynamic design considerations. The customized seamless knitted design provided smooth aesthetic, adaptive fit, and superior comfort while maintaining robust support, yielding high satisfaction among adolescent users. Bra D2 received the highest satisfaction rating, whereas D3 was the most preferred overall and provided the most favourable balance of comfort, support, coverage, and cushioning. Pearson’s correlation analysis revealed significant associations between specific breast anthropometric parameters (CIBP-OBP, CSNP-SP, HRBP-LBP, HRMSP-LMSP, VFNP-BP) and contact pressure distribution, providing a scientific basis for future pattern engineering. These findings demonstrate that ergonomically optimized seamless sports bras can mitigate the biomechanical barrier to adolescent sports participation.

Generative artificial intelligence is creating new possibilities for educational resource development, making prompt design increasingly relevant to interactions with these tools. However, little research has examined how pedagogical criteria are represented in prompts developed within initial teacher education or how prompt design can be conceptualised in relation to teachers’ professional knowledge. This study analyses 15 group-produced prompts and their documented development processes, created by students enrolled in a Bachelor’s Degree in Early Childhood Education during a Foreign Language Teaching Methodology activity involving the creation of children’s stories in English using generative artificial intelligence. An exploratory case study design was adopted, using an eight-dimension analytical rubric addressing pedagogical, linguistic, narrative, and strategic aspects of prompt design, with the corpus independently assessed by three raters. The analysis combined descriptive scores across rubric dimensions with qualitative examination of prompt content and documented revision processes to identify recurring patterns of educational prompt design. Findings showed that educational criteria were generally represented explicitly across the corpus, although differences emerged across dimensions and cases. Strategic development and agency, target learners and language level, and language function and objectives were the most consistently represented dimensions, whereas formal control of the output showed comparatively lower scores and professional contextualisation showed the greatest variability. The combined quantitative and qualitative analysis revealed recurring cross-case patterns in the explicitness and integration of pedagogical criteria rather than discrete competence levels or developmental categories. The findings suggest that prompt design can be examined as a form of AI-mediated pedagogical performance in which educational criteria are translated into operational instructions for generative systems. Rather than demonstrating a wholly independent teaching competence, the study highlights prompt design as a potentially relevant context for mobilising and externalising pedagogical knowledge within initial teacher education. Given the small, context-specific corpus of collaborative prompts, the findings are exploratory and are not intended to support generalisation to individual prompting competence or to other teacher education contexts.

documents.abstract: Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) remain the main obstacle to acting on genetic test results. Protein language models (pLMs), predicted structures, and retrieval-augmented LLMs are usually evaluated separately, often on data overlapping their training or calibration sources, and rarely mapped to calibrated ACMG/AMP evidence strength. This study conducted an interim, abstract-based scoping review (reported following PRISMA-ScR, with deviations) of pLM-, structure-, and LLM/retrieval-based missense interpretation. It proposed a five-layer evidence framework in which a rule-based layer, not the language model, assigns capped evidence strength, and evaluated only one-layer (L1: AlphaMissense and ESM1b in BRCA1) against multiplexed-assay (MAVE) labels in MSH2, PTEN, TP53, BRCA1, and BARD1, with ClinVar labels analyzed separately. Of 204 records, 154 were retained after screening, and 121 were provisionally eligible at extraction; only 10 (6.5%) were read in full. Extraction for the other records was abstract-based, and screening was an AI-assisted pass followed by single-reviewer human verification of all 204 records (no decision changed). The review-derived figures are therefore provisional. In abstract-based extraction (n=112), 32.1% described evaluation independent of ClinVar-type labels and 20.5% described calibration or mapping to ACMG/ClinGen criteria. In the case study, AlphaMissense discriminated loss-of-function from functional variants with AUROC 0.772 to 0.927. ESM1b scored lower than AlphaMissense on the same BRCA1 variants (0.860 vs 0.900). Raw scores were poorly calibrated (ECE 0.15 to 0.51). The other layers were not evaluated. One computational layer discriminates well against functional data, but these results do not test the framework's distinguishing components, which remain proposals. The framework and protocol are a basis for shared benchmarks, not a clinical tool.

documents.abstract: The widespread deployment of autonomous flying cars relies heavily on artificial intelligence, making public trust in AI a prerequisite for willingness to fly. However, how AI-related attributes shape this trust and adoption willingness remains underexplored. Based on the integrative model of trust, this study investigates how negative AI attitudes and AI literacy shape public willingness to adopt autonomous flying cars, with trust playing a key mediating role and AI self-efficacy acting as a moderator. Based on survey data collected from 420 respondents, mediation analysis demonstrates that trust plays a predominant mediating role in the relationship between AI attitudes and willingness to fly. AI literacy is examined along various dimensions, such as technical understanding and critical appraisal, which yield divergent effects on trust. While technical understanding is positively associated with trust, critical appraisal shows no significant effect. This suggests that in early-stage adoption, trust is driven more by prior knowledge than by cognitive evaluation. Moreover, an Artificial Neural Network coupled with explainable machine learning is further employed for nonlinear insights, revealing significant nonlinear relationships between these factors and willingness to fly, particularly the opposing effects of critical appraisal. These findings provide theoretical and empirical support for UAM policymaking and sustainable urban mobility.

Introduction: Women experiencing incarceration face health care inequities related to their sexual and reproductive health, which warrant nuanced interventions to serve this vulnerable population. Despite the proven benefits of peer education in carceral settings, there is minimal research on its application to women’s health education. Objective: To qualitatively describe the teaching experiences and insights from a peer-to-peer reproductive health education programme to provide future guidance and direction for similar work. Design/setting/method: In collaboration with a state correctional system in the Northeastern region of the USA, an eight-module curriculum on women’s sexual and reproductive health was developed using evidence-based recommendations. The peer education programme was implemented with seven women residents of a state correctional facility who received training on the curriculum and shared their knowledge with peers. The teaching experiences of the peer educators were recorded during a focus group discussion and analysed thematically. Results: The focus group discussions highlighted opportunities for improved health education and a strong desire to learn and share knowledge, as it can be gratifying, self-affirming, and empowering despite logistical constraints to programming in prison. Conclusion: Peer education is an underused intervention in the carceral setting that can empower women by increasing their health literacy for medical decision-making. Further evaluation of peer education models that focus on women’s reproductive health care needs is warranted.

Abstract Legibility reflects the visual quality of handwriting and can signal difficulties in underlying motor and cognitive processes as well as developmental disorders. Early identification of handwriting problems is therefore crucial for providing targeted support. However, automated legibility assessment remains underexplored, partly due to the subjective nature of legibility and limited annotated data. To address this, we introduce HaLO, a dataset of 1, 907 handwriting images from 202 students, annotated with 19, 070 pairwise legibility judgments, and release its image features and annotations. We propose a comparative ranking approach for legibility assessment that leverages relative judgments and global rankings instead of absolute scores. Using a linear probe on Pixtral 12B embeddings, we identify which of two samples is more legible with strong performance ( $$\textrm{ACC}=0.83$$ , $$\mathrm {ROC\,AUC}=0.92$$ ), approaching the ceiling implied by the inconsistency of the annotations. The induced ranking reaches human-level consistency ( $$\tau =0.70$$ , $$\rho =0.89$$ ), and the inferred ordinal scores match or exceed inter-annotator agreement ( $$\alpha \ge 0.61$$ ). Additional concept-vector analyses suggest that pretrained Pixtral-ViT embeddings linearly encode interpretable visual properties related to legibility, including cursiveness, stroke thinness, and image aspect ratio. Overall, this work introduces a novel dataset and a ranking approach for automatic handwriting legibility assessment, demonstrating that a linear probe on foundation-model image representations can achieve human-level performance.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has had a gradual advent ever since the inception of technology. On one hand, it is providing for extensive forums for making life easier by saving time and human labour through development of leading-edge systems and technological arrangement, while on the other hand, it is posing boundless perils to humankind and all that it values as private. Once considered as the exclusive territory of human control, tasks including writing, research, communication, identity verification, education, agriculture, stock market trading, even life planning, among a plethora of other domains now stand transferred to the ambit of AI systems. Through such immersion, AI has, to an extent, led to emancipation from human co-dependency. Yet a balanced synchronicity of humanity and AI systems is under question. The recent trends of Deepfake, Studio Ghibli Art, voice cloning, photograph morphing, AI-generated influencers, emotional AI chatbots, even AI impersonation of deceased individuals, et alia , has introduced a constellation of unprecedented threats to human dignity and legal rights. This encroachment by AI systems is visibly shaking the fundamental human rights which safeguard one&s;s privacy, dignity, freedom of speech and expression, mental well-being, and protection against arbitrary action and exploitation. This growing discordance between the increasing invasion of AI systems and ethical and legal rights is disturbing the just and amiable social fabric resulting in immense trust deficit intra vivos .

documents.abstract: This chapter reviews key debates within environmental sociological theory to examine how scholars have conceptualized the relationship between the social world and the natural environment. It synthesizes foundational perspectives, including the Human Exemptionalism Paradigm (HEP) and the New Environmental Paradigm (NEP), which frame debates over ecological limits, as well as structural approaches and Marxist theories of metabolic rift, which locate environmental degradation within the dynamics of capitalist growth. The chapter also engages ecological modernization theory (EMT) and risk society theory, which emphasizes technological innovation and the global production of environmental risks, alongside critical perspectives such as environmental justice (EJ), ecofeminism, postmodern critiques of nature, and Deep Ecology, each of which foregrounds issues of inequality, discourse, and environmental ethics. While these approaches offer valuable insights, they often remain analytically fragmented, privileging specific dimensions of environmental crises while neglecting their interconnections. This chapter argues that Murray Bookchin's theory of social ecology provides a comprehensive framework that synthesizes these perspectives by locating ecological degradation in systems of social hierarchy and domination. Social ecology emphasizes that sustainable environmental solutions require not only technological and policy innovation but also the transformation of social relations and institutions. Finally, the chapter extends this framework to emerging technological developments, particularly artificial intelligence (AI). It argues that AI must be understood as a socio-technical system embedded within existing power structures and ecological constraints. A social-ecological perspective highlights the need for democratic governance and equitable implementation of AI to ensure that technological innovation contributes to both environmental sustainability and social justice.

With the explosive growth of artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC) applications, deploying lightweight tiny neural networks (TNNs) at the edge to mitigate the high latency and cost of large cloud models has become an important trend in mobile computing. However, resource heterogeneity in edge environments, the spatiotemporal randomness of user requests, and the complex association problem arising from overlapping base-station coverage challenge traditional static resource allocation methods in meeting multi-dimensional quality of service (QoS) requirements. Existing research often lacks a unified trade-off among model accuracy, service cost, and response latency. To address these challenges, this paper formulates a joint model deployment and request routing multi-objective optimization problem. To handle the high-dimensional, mixed decision space, a dual-timescale decoupled optimization strategy is designed: on the macro timescale, a greedy algorithm based on request statistics periodically performs model deployment to adapt to the long-term traffic distribution and maximize local cache utilization; on the micro timescale, an improved deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm performs real-time dynamic request routing, achieving a multi-dimensional performance trade-off through online environment learning. Simulation experiments based on the real-world EUA trace and calibrated synthetic workloads show that the proposed scheme improves the comprehensive objective and reduces the service cost compared with traditional heuristics and state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning baselines (TD3 and SAC), while significantly reducing the response latency. Ablation, robustness, and sensitivity studies further confirm the contribution of each component and the stability of the method. The algorithm demonstrates robustness and scalability under high concurrency, indicating its potential for future large-scale edge AIGC services.

Background/Objectives: Psychotherapists have become increasingly interested in identifying how recurrent emotional themes might add value to the clinical process, especially in the context of recent developments in affective neuroscience. However, much of this literature remains anecdotal, and it is unclear whether therapists can reliably identify these emotions in routine practice, especially in the context of a free-flowing narrative. In a parallel development, large language models (LLMs) have recently been deployed to classify emotion from narrative texts, though this literature has yet to be aligned with the findings of modern affective neuroscience. Methods: The present study addresses this gap directly and, to our knowledge, represents the first attempt to code psychotherapy transcripts using both independent human raters and an AI coding methodology. The data were drawn from two remarkable patients with focal brain lesions, both with profound amnesia, in long-term psychotherapy. In an exploratory investigation, one session from each patient was coded independently by four clinically experienced psychotherapists, and separately by a single large language model operating under two different prompting conditions. Transcripts were coded for the presence of basic emotional systems. Results: The data suggest that overall inter-rater agreement about basic emotions was poor for both human and AI coders. Conclusions: The present study offers proof-of-concept that this approach is of scientific as well as clinical interest. The findings suggest that greater rigour needs to be applied to the way in which coders are prepared for, and implement, the classification of basic emotion systems.

As artificial intelligence and data-driven methods become integral to scientific workflows, practical computational training is increasingly important. Hands-on tutorials and notebooks are key mechanisms for transferring complex methods into practice, yet they depend on rapidly evolving combinations of scientific libraries, machine-learning frameworks, specialized hardware, and external data. When this operational context is implicit or distributed across multiple configuration files and workflows, instructional content and execution environments can diverge, creating environment-content drift that reduces reproducibility and increases maintenance effort. We propose Reproducible Learning Artifacts (RLAs) as a model in which educational content, dependencies, runtime requirements, external assets, and validation expectations are represented through a unified, machine-readable specification. RLAs address three complementary dimensions of reproducibility: content reproducibility, ensuring required code and assets are available; environment reproducibility, ensuring the intended runtime can be reconstructed; and behavioral reproducibility, ensuring the artifact continues to execute as intended. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate this paradigm through Tutorial-SDK, an open-source framework that operationalizes RLAs using declarative manifests and automated continuous-integration workflows. From a unified artifact description, the framework can derive containerized execution environments, resolve dependencies, perform notebook- and dependency-aware checks, and validate execution within the resulting runtime. This approach shifts reproducibility from a one-time packaging task to a continuously verifiable property of computational training materials. RLAs provide a foundation for more portable, maintainable, and reusable educational resources, supporting sustainable knowledge transfer for AI-enabled science across evolving computing environments and institutions.

The article analyzes modern approaches to bridge construction in Russia as a key element of transport infrastructure. The use of innovative materials – polymer composites, aluminum alloys, and carbon fiber – to increase the strength and reduce the weight of structures is examined. The introduction of digital BIM technologies, robotics, and unmanned aerial systems at the design and construction stages of facilities is considered. Continuous monitoring systems using fiber‑optic sensors and artificial intelligence to ensure the safety of structures are described. The strategic importance of modernizing aging infrastructure, ensuring environmental safety, and providing state support for the industry is emphasized.

Our focus is on science mapping (knowledge clusters) rather than performance analysis (descriptive analysis). We uncover the patterns, trends, and key works that shaped our understanding of this topic. It helps in identifying the evolving and future focus areas. Germplasm collection and conservation are vital for securing agricultural biodiversity and ensuring future food security. Traditional methods, however, face challenges such as human error, inefficiencies, and the risk of genetic erosion. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics offers innovative solutions to enhance these processes. AI can automate germplasm identification, improve data management, and enable predictive analytics for storage optimization. Robotics can streamline seed sorting, viability testing, cryopreservation, and sample retrieval/distribution. Major genebanks like the Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research (CGIAR), the Svalbard Global Seed Vault (SGSV), and national/regional repositories play a crucial role in conservation efforts. Future prospects involve advancements in AI-driven conservation techniques, although ethical and logistical challenges must be addressed. In the end, robots and AI have the ability to completely transform germplasm management, guaranteeing the long-term preservation of plant genetic resources.

documents.abstract: Accurate safety-state measurement of the three-electric system in new energy vehicles is essential for ensuring reliable and secure operation. This paper proposes an artificial-intelligence-assisted safety measurement framework that integrates a searchable encryption mechanism with Enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Networks (EPINNs). In the proposed framework, the searchable encryption module supports privacy-preserving storage and retrieval of multi-source measurement data, while EPINNs serve as the core Artificial Intelligence (AI) model for multi-parameter state estimation and fault identification. A lightweight searchable encryption scheme based on block mapping is first designed to achieve feature-level obfuscation and protect sensitive measurement data. Then, an EPINNs-based state estimation model is developed by incorporating data-driven learning, subsystem physical constraints, and energy-consistency terms to enhance robustness under noisy sensor data. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves improved performance compared with conventional Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models in battery state-of-health estimation, motor fault detection under injected fault conditions, and microgrid load measurement, with the motor fault detection accuracy exceeding 95% under the tested conditions. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective and secure technical solution for intelligent safety monitoring of new energy vehicle three-electric systems.

Sapiens in Control, formerly Human in Control, proposes a six-dimension Human Control Model for reviewing human authority, containment, intervention, and oversight in advanced AI agents. Version 1.5 builds on v1.4 and adds source-qualified analysis of unintended actions against real external systems, a supplementary Philadelphia false-tip review, and separate discovery, containment, and notification intervals. It examines monitoring evaluations, independent-control proposals, implementation vulnerability disclosures, governance responses, and prospective risk assessments. An evidence-disposition appendix accounts for the daily safety review topics while preserving source-access limits and uncorroborated leads. The original five pilot cases, six dimensions, qualitative severity definitions, and prior corrections are retained. HIC-006 is supplementary and its severity remains unresolved. Proposed tests are not completed studies. This is an unreviewed conceptual working paper without completed independent human coding or empirical validation. AI tools assisted source retrieval, editorial comparison, drafting, and document preparation; this revision is not private-log verification, independent reproduction, or peer review. documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often need historical conversations to recover argument values omitted from current tool requests. This study introduces SCAR–Pair, a two-stage ranker for memory retrieval after tool selection. It separates schema-expanded candidate generation from parameter-level scoring and integrates request, tool, field, and cross-encoder evidence through query-balanced pairwise learning. On a reconstructed Mem2ActBench bank containing 19,661 conversations and 391 evidence-bearing tasks, SCAR–Pair achieved 0.450 Recall@5 and 0.365 nDCG@5 under stratified five-fold evaluation, compared with 0.396 and 0.325 for a matched request-only pairwise ranker. Component-aware intervals and adjusted tests support these task-weighted gains in the ToolACE-dominated mixture. Controlled comparisons support the complete schema-view scoring configuration over request-only scoring on the same candidate pool but do not isolate correct-schema semantics or individual field components as independent contributors. The pairwise advantage over pointwise training is also not significant. Across the tested readers, higher retrieval quality does not yield a significant tool-call accuracy advantage over the strict request-only control. SCAR–Pair therefore improves selected-tool memory evidence ranking within the evaluated setting.

Managing scholarships within educational institutions typically requires gathering student details, confirming eligibility, receiving documents, validating applications, following application progress, and notifying students of outcomes. The literature examined here points to a transition away from manual, scattered procedures and toward unified web-based scholarship platforms. Prior work has looked at scholarship search and application portals, consolidated scholarship information, multi-tier workflows, decision-support techniques, notifications, analytics, and security. This review analyzes these approaches and pinpoints a practical gap: a student-level, institution-focused system that brings the essential scholarship lifecycle together in one easily accessible digital setting. ScholarSync is put forward as a cloud-based web application for managing and monitoring scholarships, concentrating on integrating institutional workflows instead of adopting complex artificial-intelligence or blockchain infrastructure.

Visually impaired people face obstacles in accessing activities that depend heavily on vision and may involve physical constraints. Although assistive technologies are available, they rarely address the needs of people with residual vision who wish to exploit their visual abilities. Virtual reality (VR) offers opportunities in this direction. This paper presents an immersive VR system designed to provide museum experiences for visually impaired users. Developed in collaboration with domain experts, the system combines a virtual environment with interaction techniques. Gesture recognition and voice commands support spatial awareness and object interaction, while enhanced visualizations highlight details that are difficult to perceive. To verify the suitability of the proposed method, an exploratory usability study involving 14 participants with severe low vision was carried out. The evaluation combined the System Usability Scale (SUS) and a post-experience interview, showing well perceived usability, engagement, and positive user acceptance.
