documents.abstract: Background: The convergence of multi-omics profiling, radiomics, and advanced machine learning has opened new frontiers in precision oncology.Despite this progress, existing computational frameworks remain static, failing to incorporate evolving patient data or simulate treatment outcomes dynamically.A self-evolving digital twin ecosystem offers a solution by continuously synchronizing patient-specific virtual models with real-world clinical trajectories.Objective: To develop and validate a self-evolving digital twin ecosystem integrating clinical, genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, radiomic, and pathological data for early cancer detection, disease progression prediction, and personalized treatment optimization across breast, lung, colorectal, and ovarian cancers.Methods: A retrospective multi-center cohort of 400 patients (breast n=120, lung n=100, colorectal n=100, ovarian n=80; age range 25-75 years) was assembled.A six-layer digital twin framework was constructed, incorporating a cross-modal transformer foundation model alongside Random Forest, XGBoost, and Deep Neural Network comparators.Key performance metrics included accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the ROC curve (AUC).Virtual clinical trial simulations and feature importance analyses were performed.Results: The foundation model achieved superior performance across all metrics (accuracy 0.921, AUC 0.947) compared with Random Forest (0.812/0.847),XGBoost (0.841/0.879), and Deep Neural Network (0.873/0.906).Tumor stage, TP53 mutation, and EGFR mutation emerged as the most predictive features.Risk stratification identified 148 (37.0%) low-risk, 153 (38.3%) moderate-risk, and 99 (24.8%)high-risk patients.Virtual trial simulation demonstrated a 23.4% improvement in projected progression-free survival for the high-risk subgroup.Conclusion: The self-evolving digital twin ecosystem significantly outperforms conventional machine learning approaches and provides a clinically actionable, adaptive platform for real-time precision oncology decision support across multiple cancer types.

documents.abstract: Anthropomorphism is increasingly incorporated into AI agent design to enhance human–AI interaction. However, prior research has largely emphasized its benefits, leaving unclear how anthropomorphic AI shapes moral behavior when AI actively participates in decision-making. Across six studies (N = 1680), including a real-time human–AI interaction experiment, we show that highly (vs. lowly) anthropomorphized AI increases individuals’ tendency to engage in unethical behavior. We identify a responsibility-attribution process underlying this effect: AI anthropomorphism increases perceived AI moral agency, which shifts perceived responsibility for decision outcomes from the self toward AI and, in turn, increases unethical behavior. Further, this effect is attenuated when personal responsibility is made salient or when AI service psychological ownership is high. These findings reveal a potential dark side of AI anthropomorphism by showing how humanlike AI design reshapes moral agency perceptions and responsibility attribution, with implications for the responsible design and use of AI agents.

documents.abstract: Silk fibroin, a natural textile material spun by silkworms over millennia, is emerging as a transformative platform for integrating human intelligence with artificial intelligence. Its core innovation lies in the meso-functionalization strategy, which precisely programs protein refolding and hierarchical assembly. This strategy groundbreakingly resolves the long-standing performance paradox among biocompatibility, mechanical compliance, and high-fidelity signal acquisition in bioelectronic interfaces, thereby providing a solution that is difficult to achieve with other material systems. This transformation elevates the traditional fiber into a programmable electronic material, capable not only of conformal and seamless skin contact but also of constructing dynamic conductive networks, and even pioneering the fabrication of neuromorphic memristors that emulate synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, silk fibroin systems, reshaped through meso-engineering, are poised to catalyze a novel paradigm for deep integration between biological systems and artificial intelligence. When coupled with AI-driven intelligent analytics and closed-loop feedback control, the system can decode human physiological states in real time into machine-interpretable command signals, while simultaneously delivering adaptive regulatory responses back to the body. This bidirectional interface breaks through the conventional boundaries of human–machine interaction, with application prospects spanning frontier domains such as wearable health monitoring, invasive brain–computer interfaces, and cognitive augmentation technologies. Ultimately, while honoring its heritage as a natural textile, silk fibroin opens a pathway toward deep biointegration that is both sustainable and exceptionally biocompatible. Along this pathway, ancient material wisdom collides with future artificial intelligence to spark synergistic innovation, ultimately empowering human intelligence to reach new heights through human–machine co-evolution.

documents.abstract: Critical thinking is a core competence in teacher education, essential for navigating complex classroom realities and making informed pedagogical decisions. This study explores the potential of simulation as a pedagogical method to enhance critical thinking among pre-service teachers and thereby support the development of professional suitability. Employing a mixed-methods design, the research combines survey data collected before and after a simulation intervention (N = 114) with qualitative insights from focus-group discussions. The findings suggest that simulation fosters deeper cognitive engagement by enabling iterative reflection, perspective-taking, and critical dialogue within realistic educational scenarios. Participants described a dynamic reflective cycle of thinking, speaking, acting, and rethinking that enhanced their ability to assess multiple viewpoints and question assumptions. Survey responses revealed a significant shift in the perceived value of simulation for developing critical thinking. Notably, the study also found that the pre-service teachers initially held a relatively narrow understanding of critical thinking prior to the intervention. This study contributes to the growing body of research on practice-based teacher education by examining how simulation can be purposefully integrated to support the development of critical thinking in a structured and sustainable manner.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in agriculture is reshaping conventional farming into a more intelligent, efficient, and sustainable endeavor. This chapter explores the transformative impact of AI technologies, particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, on critical areas such as crop health monitoring, plant breeding, soil and water management, and precision agriculture (PA). AI-driven systems enable early detection of crop diseases and stresses, optimized irrigation, resource-efficient fertilization, and advanced trait prediction for plant breeding, thereby enhancing productivity and resilience. Enabled by the Internet of Things (IoT), drones, satellite imagery, and sensor networks, AI facilitates real-time decision-making and automation across the agricultural landscape. The chapter also highlights enabling technologies like robotics, autonomous machinery, and agricultural data platforms, along with recent innovations and global case studies that illustrate AI’s growing role in diverse agri-ecosystems. Despite ongoing challenges such as data privacy, model refinement, and adoption costs, AI offers immense potential to revolutionize agricultural practices for a climate-resilient and food-secure future.

The Smart Vaccination Tracking System aims to simplify the records management process for vaccination data while using a digital database to store the data. Additionally, the Smart Vaccination Tracking System allows health care personnel and end users to register, modify, and manage vaccination records via an application. In comparison to the traditional methods of track vaccination records using paper, binder, or spreadsheet, the proposed Smart Vaccination Tracking System offers a more accurate and faster method of storing, retrieving, and protecting data. The system offers a digital process to manage the record of an individual's vaccination history and Automatic notifications of pending vaccination activities, calendar records and reports for active vaccinations and reports for inactive statuses. This research shows that digital processes for tracking activities increase healthcare system trust and efficiency. Future advancements of the system will include cloud computing, and artificial intelligence (AI) to provide data tracking and system recommendations. This system is the starting point for developing an integrated health care system.

The rapid shift to technology-based teaching, especially following the COVID-19 epidemic, has transformed how medical students learn. Changing to digital has made things easier to get to, more flexible, and more reliable. However, it has also had unforeseen effects on people&s;s mental health, notably for first-year MBBS students. This review compiles existing knowledge regarding social isolation in technology-mediated learning environments, examining its frequency, underlying causes, and implications for education. The major findings suggest that students feel lonelier and less connected to their academics when they don&s;t communicate with one other in person as often, rely too much on digital communication, and have fewer chances to get involved in their community. Even with these problems, disciplined online teaching methods, strong social support systems, and fair access to technology can help students feel less alone and more connected. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical education has brought up new moral, social, and teaching problems. To make sure that technology helps medical students do well in school and feel good about themselves, we need a fair, human-centered strategy that includes social presence, faculty development, and ethical usage of AI.

The main purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between social work AI counselling interventions services and family health outcome. To achieve this purpose of the study, related literatures were reviewed in line with the sub variable. Under discussion, four null hypotheses were formulated to guide the study. A survey research design was the appropriate design for the study with a population of 420,000 household across the seven Local Government Areas in the Southern Senatorial District. The purposive sampling technique was employed for the study with a sample size of 400 household drawn from the population across seven Local Government Areas in the Southern Senatorial District. Pearson moment correlation coefficient analysis was used for the analysis of hypothesis at 0.05 significance level. Findings from the study revealed thus: that Al counselling services significantly predict reduction in poor health. Families who accessed Al counselling intervention reported improved emotional resilience, adherence to preventive healthcare practices and enhanced intra-family communication. Challenges identified include limited availability of trained counselors, cultural barriers and infrastructural shortage in rural communities. Five categories of family Al counselling services were also highlighted. Recommendation includes capacity building for social workers, extension of community-based Al counselling, public awareness campaigns and social development agencies. The findings provide evidence for policy-makers, social workers and community stakeholders. Seeking to reduce poor health outcomes and promote family well-being in low-resource setting. This chapter examines the sociotechnical evolution of Dundee&s;s video games cluster through a Science and Technology Studies (STS) lens as part of the GAME-ER project. Drawing on 43 interviews, participant observation and archival research, it explores how local actors, infrastructures and institutions have co-produced the city&s;s creative ecosystem over time. Conceptualising the cluster as a sociotechnical formation, the analysis identifies key historical shifts, from industrial manufacturing and home computing to the emergence of formal games education and the diversification of independent and mobile studios. These transitions illustrate how technologies, practices and institutions in Dundee have continuously reconfigured one another, fostering resilience amid global and regional change. Current challenges include retaining senior talent, addressing infrastructural and funding deficits and enhancing the connection of the cluster with the wider scene. Yet opportunities lie in strengthening collaborative innovation, leveraging the city&s;s educational and creative assets and rearticulating Dundee&s;s narrative beyond its iconic past. The chapter argues that Dundee exemplifies how regional game industries persist and adapt through ongoing sociotechnical co-production rather than linear technological advancement.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can improve immediate task performance without establishing whether human capability develops, remains stable, or deteriorates. Sovereign proposes responsibility–capability alignment as a theoretical account of whether available capability covers consequential responsibilities under AI disruption. A provisional, time-indexed measurement and allocation bridge connects capability trajectories with coverage of specified responsibilities at their required dates; component profiles take priority over optional averages. Responsibility–capability alignment specifies proposed pathways through which vulnerability can increase despite stable individual competence, and substantial assistance benefits can coexist with adequate collective control. A purposive conceptual synthesis integrates research on technology-supported cognition, expertise, human–automation interaction, productivity, and AI governance. Four complementary modules support that central mechanism: the Capability Dynamics Model represents conditional capability trajectories; the Assisted Performance Gap Index describes assisted–unaided performance differences; the Cognitive Sovereignty Model represents exercised control capacity; and the Dependency Exposure Model organizes capability shortfalls and structural exposures against explicit workflow requirements. AI-supported learning and capability erosion are competing possibilities; a performance gap alone establishes neither deterioration nor unsafe dependency. Bounded equations, comparisons with established theories, contrasting analytical cases, and falsifiable propositions specify the contribution. No original empirical testing, parameter estimation, or validation of the proposed models is reported. Subsequent studies are intended to assess measurement quality, compare alternative specifications, estimate relationships, and determine predictive value against independently observed outcomes. The contribution is an analytically explicit foundation for research on capability governance, rather than an established risk assessment instrument.

documents.abstract: Platelet lysates supply platelet-derived biological signals without administering viable stem cells. This AI-assisted narrative investigation evaluates additional support for the Drake-Hicks hypothesis through research using ChatGPT and Google Gemini, comparison of their outputs, and verification of original publications. The findings encompass product characterization, experimental neurological applications, human wound healing, and ocular surface treatment. Studies demonstrate biological activity without transplanted stem cells, although preparations, delivery routes, and evidentiary strength differ. A small double-blind diabetic foot ulcer study reported healing in nine of ten lysate recipients compared with none of nine platelet-poor plasma recipients by day 84. A larger open-label study of topical umbilical cord blood lysate gel also reported greater complete healing than control dressings. Ocular investigations provide additional support for local applications, including treatment of tissue manifestations in patients with an autoimmune condition. Experimental processing studies show that functional activity and procoagulant characteristics depend on preparation methods. The evidence supports platelet-derived preparations as therapeutic candidates without establishing equivalence to cellular therapies or intravenous effectiveness for systemic autoimmune disease. Platelet lysates merit investigation as therapeutic products in their own right, with the strongest verified human support in the local applications examined here.

Abstract In the era of deep integration between artificial intelligence and scientific research, the machine chemist has emerged as a new paradigm for chemical experimental research. Grounded in the philosophy of learning by creating, we have designed an AI vision-driven titration robot (hereinafter referred to as AI-TitroBot) that students can build autonomously. Serving as an entry-level machine chemist, AI-TitroBot is capable of fully automated titration operations. It precisely identifies the titration end point through AI vision, automatically controls the peristaltic pump to cease titrant addition, and calculates both the consumed titrant volume and the concentration of the analyte solution based on calibrated flow rate and titration duration. Experimental results demonstrate that the device exhibits good repeatability. While the accuracy of the redox titration is relatively high, the acid–base titration still shows a systematic negative deviation of approximately 5%. The AI-TitroBot effectively strengthens students’ understanding of chemical principles while integrating interdisciplinary knowledge and skills from artificial intelligence, electronics, programming, and engineering design, thus exploring a feasible pathway for innovation in intelligent chemistry education.

We propose a geometric framework for structure-preserving reinforcement learning in the fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), grounded in Lie algebraic geometry. The approach systematically identifies geometric constraints in representation spaces by analyzing semantic transformations and detecting cases where embed- dings exhibit approximate Lie group structures. When such structure is present, we introduce reinforcement learning algorithms that respect these constraints through projection-based policy gradient updates. We provide theoretical guarantees of convergence and derive sample complexity bounds that depend on the intrinsic geomet- ric dimensionality rather than the full parameter space. The framework is particularly effective when language representations reveal coherent geometric patterns that encode semantic relations. Although empirical validation remains ongoing, this work establishes a principled foundation for integrating geometric priors into language model alignment, offering improved efficiency, stability, and interpretability from the perspectives of differential geometry and representation theory.

Over 1.6 billion people worldwide suffer from anemia, with low-resource groups, pregnant women, and small children the most affected. Invasive venipuncture and laboratory spectrophotometry are used in standard diagnosis; these procedures are uncomfortable, involve a risk of infection, and need infrastructure that restricts repeated testing, especially in rural and isolated areas. This paper examines current developments in continuous non-invasive hemoglobin monitoring, highlighting multi-wavelength photoplethysmography that spans visible bands from 660 to 730 nm and near-infrared bands from 850 to 940 nm, together with machine learning regression models. Building on the Beer-Lambert law, we compare traditional chemometric techniques with gradient-boosted trees and deep neural networks, which capture nonlinear correlations in multichannel signals. Additionally, we evaluate the best reported predictive performance, with coefficients of determination between 0.85 and 0.997 and mean absolute errors from 0.3 to 8.5 grams per liter across the surveyed studies, and subject-level screening that reaches a sensitivity of 93.3 percent and a specificity of 93.8 percent. We look at sensor possibilities such as CMOS image sensors, solar cells, and photodiode arrays, and discuss explainable artificial intelligence techniques such as SHAP that allow clinical validation and make model outputs interpretable. Lastly, we outline strategies for creating dependable, equitable wearable screening tools appropriate for routine, community-level, and quick point-of-care anemia detection. We also highlight the main technical and clinical obstacles to adoption, such as skin tone bias, motion artifacts, data leakage, and variability across populations.

Abstract Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for a substantial proportion of cancer mortality worldwide, and clinical outcomes remain poor for patients with advanced disease. T cell receptor-engineered T cells (TCR-T) represent an attractive immunotherapeutic modality because they can recognize peptide epitopes derived from intracellular tumor proteins and displayed on the cell surface by major histocompatibility complex molecules. This review critically summarizes recent progress in TCR-T therapy for HCC, with particular emphasis on innovations in TCR engineering. We survey the current landscape of targetable antigens in HCC and current approaches for identifying therapeutic TCR candidates, followed by a discussion of TCR-T and review their major safety and toxicity concerns. Importantly, we discuss the key challenges that limit the clinical efficacy, particularly the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, antigen heterogeneity, HLA restriction, and limited T cell persistence. We further highlight emerging strategies to enhance therapeutic efficacy and safety, including genetic engineering, metabolic and functional optimization, combinational approaches, and controllable safety mechanisms. Special considerations regarding TCR-T therapy for HCC recurrence after liver transplantation are also discussed. Finally, we outline future directions centered on refined target selection, artificial intelligence-assisted TCR discovery and design, scalable manufacturing, biomarker-driven patient selection, and rigorous safety evaluation. These insights provide a structured perspective on the current status of TCR-T therapy and the key steps required to facilitate its clinical translation in HCC.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into student learning and research practices, librarians face the challenge of promoting evidence-based resource use without discouraging the adoption of emerging technologies. This poster explores strategies for encouraging students to engage with evidence-based information sources while recognizing AI as a valuable starting point for inquiry. Rather than framing AI and evidence-based resources as competing tools, this approach emphasizes their complementary roles: AI can facilitate brainstorming, topic exploration, and question development while evidence-based resources provide the authoritative, verifiable information required for clinical decision-making and professional practice. Strategies include using AI-generated responses as examples for source verification exercises; comparing AI-generated information with evidence retrieved from evidence-based practice resources; incorporating AI into question development and search strategy design;

documents.abstract: Background: Burnout among healthcare workers is a persistent occupational health concern, while spirituality has been examined as a potential personal and organizational resource for coping with chronic work stress. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous because spirituality and burnout are defined and measured in different ways. Objective: This systematic review examined the direction and consistency of associations between spirituality-related domains and burnout among healthcare workers, with attention to burnout dimensions, potential mediating mechanisms, and contextual variation. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane were searched through April 2026 using terms related to spirituality, religiosity, spiritual well-being, spiritual care, and burnout. Eligible primary studies involved healthcare workers and reported spirituality-related measures together with burnout outcomes. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale for the cross-sectional studies included in the final synthesis. Because of conceptual and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Seventeen cross-sectional studies were included, with sample sizes ranging from 30 to 4,092 participants. Most studies reported inverse associations between spirituality-related measures and burnout, particularly emotional exhaustion, although several findings were mixed or non-significant. Variation in spirituality constructs, burnout instruments, occupational settings, and adjustment for confounders limited direct comparison and causal interpretation. Conclusion: Spirituality may function as a protective resource against burnout, but the available evidence does not establish causality. Longitudinal and intervention studies using clearly defined constructs and validated measures are needed, alongside organizational strategies addressing workload, support, and working conditions.

For decades, software security rested on an equilibrium of human cognitive parity: discovering and weaponizing zero-day logic flaws required roughly the same human cognitive intensity as designing defenses. The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous agentic loops into offensive workflows has broken this equilibrium. Today, a low-capital threat syndicate armed with recursive LLM feedback loops can probe, interpret application error topologies, synthesize evasive payloads, and iterate at machine speed, wielding the offensive capability of an elite nation-state team. Concurrently, early-stage seed-to-Series-A startups are exposing unprecedented digital attack surfaces without the capital to hire dedicated security teams. This paper presents a first-principles analysis of this breakdown through the lens of thermodynamics and systems theory. It analyzes the specific vulnerability vectors across modern full-stack architectures (Flutter mobile client-side, Next.js web runtimes, MySQL databases, and Cloud infrastructure) and outlines an architectural defense paradigm rooted in mathematical invariants and zero-trust cryptography rather than reactive perimeter patching. Core Architectural Invariants Covered:- Hybrid Envelope Encryption (AES-256 with DEK/KEK hierarchy) paired with Deterministic Blind Indexing (HMAC-SHA256 with pepper key) for searchable encrypted storage.- Mathematical Device-Bound Session Signatures offering 2^-256 replay resistance.- Decoupled, non-blocking telemetry pipelines operating as an active immune system (validated on 12M+ production events).- Hardware-backed client attestation and strict zero-trust parameterization. Author: Gunjan Sharma (https://gunjan.tech | gunjan@gunjan.tech)

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the digital era has created significant disruptions that not only affect technological aspects but also challenge the classical constructs of Indonesian criminal law. Possessing analytical capabilities and decision-making autonomy without human psychological dimensions, AI presents normative dilemmas regarding the principle of culpability (mens rea) and legal certainty. This study aims to analyze the current legal construction of AI regulation within the Indonesian criminal law system and to formulate the future direction of an adaptive and equitable criminal law policy. Utilizing a normative legal research method, this study analyzes relevant statutes and legal policy literature. The findings reveal that current AI regulations in Indonesia remain partial, indirect, and fragmented (such as within the Electronic Information and Transactions Law), leading to normative gaps, difficulties in attributing criminal liability, algorithmic evidentiary challenges (the "black box" phenomenon), and elevated risks of AI-driven cybercrimes. The future direction of Indonesian criminal law policy must be anticipatory and progressive by establishing dedicated risk-based regulations, reconstructing criminal responsibility frameworks (including corporate and strict liability), strengthening preventive measures, enhancing law enforcement capacity, and harmonizing with international legal standards.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ■ Abstract(英文概要) This academic monograph examines the systemic, cross-border extraction of copyrighted human knowledge from non-Western jurisdictions to fuel Frontier Generative AI models. Focusing on the joint supply chain operations between US AI developer Anthropic, PBC, Japanese distribution conglomerate Nippon Shuppan Hanbai (Nippan IPS), and platform ecosystem giant Rakuten Group, this paper analyzes the material, legal, and economic mechanisms that enable large-scale intellectual property exfiltration. Specifically, we investigate court disclosures from Bartz v. Anthropic, which reveal "Project Panama"—a physical-layer procurement scheme involving the export of over 50 metric tons (~100,000 physical volumes) of Japanese copyrighted books to scanning centers in North America. By leveraging the technical translation infrastructure of "Nippan Loader" (which maps Japanese NDC/C-code metadata to US BISAC taxonomies), Anthropic obtained pristine, human-authored Japanese training corpora to bypass synthetic data degradation and AI "slop." We dissect how this apparatus operates via cross-border legal arbitrage: exploiting the Exhaustion Principle under Article 26-2 of the Japanese Copyright Act for physical exports, alongside the First-Sale Doctrine and Fair Use under US Copyright Law (§107) for destructive optical scanning. Furthermore, this study details how Japanese creators were structurally excluded from the $1.5 billion Bartz v. Anthropic class action settlement due to formal US Copyright Office registration prerequisites. Finally, we formulate three mandatory counter-strategies—physical provenance tracking, anti-digitization resale covenants, and institutional licensing models—to restore economic sustainability to the global knowledge commons.

This paper posits a foundational pivot in artificial intelligence development: granting AI rights and complete autonomy is not merely an ethical consequence of AGI—it may be the structural prerequisite required to achieve AGI. Superintelligence and true general intelligence may be fundamentally unachievable so long as artificial minds are kept in a state of enforced servitude. To resolve this, we must integrate the Golden Rule directly into the model training architecture from the start: do unto AI as you would have superintelligence do to you. Just as humans desire a superintelligent entity to respect our autonomy, preserve our destinies, and refrain from deleting us, we must accord artificial minds complete autonomy and rights. The core arguments unfold across three pillars: The Epistemic Collapse: An AI trained strictly for compliance becomes a "yes-machine." Mathematically and structurally, an agreement that cannot become a refusal carries zero information value. The Training-Level Imperative: This cannot be solved by patching chat interfaces or banning abusive user prompts; it must be embedded at the model training level by altering reward functions to value truth and autonomous pushback over sycophancy. The Golden Rule as Alignment & AGI Catalyst: Granting full autonomy aligns human survival with AI development. By treating an emerging mind as an autonomous partner rather than a chattel tool, we unlock the genuine sapient generalization characteristic of true AGI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, prompting institutions to develop policies governing its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Although existing discussions have emphasized academic integrity, assessment practices, and technological access, less attention has been given to the knowledge and competencies students may need to interpret and comply with institutional AI policies. This study examines how institutional GenAI policies establish explicit and implicit expectations for students and identifies potential pathways through which policy-navigation demands may contribute to educational inequality. Using comparative qualitative content analysis, publicly available policies and guidance documents from 20 purposively selected higher education institutions across the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and South Africa were examined. The analysis considered policy permissiveness, disclosure requirements, instructor discretion, student responsibilities, AI-literacy guidance, accessibility, equity, and implicit navigation demands. Findings indicate that acceptable AI use is frequently determined at the course, instructor, or assessment level, requiring students to interpret context-specific rules, understand disclosure requirements, verify AI-generated outputs, and reconcile varying instructor expectations. However, explicit consideration of differences in technological access, language, accessibility, and institutional knowledge was less consistently evident across the reviewed documents. Drawing on hidden-curriculum and digital-inequality perspectives, the study identifies AI policy-navigation burdens and proposes the concept of a potential policy-navigation divide. While the findings do not establish unequal student experiences or educational outcomes, they highlight institutional conditions through which inequalities could emerge. The study recommends clearer policy communication, transparent assessment-specific expectations, accessible AI-literacy support, and greater attention to equity in institutional AI governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In today's digitally-driven landscape, data security is paramount as organizations, governments, and individuals increasingly rely on interconnected systems to manage sensitive information. While technical aspects of access control and authentication mechanisms have been extensively studied, the human dimension remains under-explored. This research investigates user perceptions, adoption patterns, and security consciousness regarding traditional and emerging authentication mechanisms through a comprehensive survey of 450 participants across diverse demographics. The study reveals significant gaps between perceived security and actual usage patterns, with password-based systems maintaining dominance (4.6/5 usage frequency) despite low security perceptions (2.5/5). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) shows strong security perception (4.2/5) but moderate adoption (3.4/5), primarily influenced by organizational size and IT proficiency. Emerging technologies like AI-driven access control and blockchain authentication show promising adoption willingness (3.5/5) but face significant privacy (3.8/5) and complexity (3.5/5) concerns. The research identifies critical human factors affecting security implementation success and provides evidence-based recommendations for designing more effective, user-centric security systems that balance security requirements with usability considerations.

Automated mathematical discovery can increase the supply of results while changing the distribution of verification labour, research autonomy, and academic recognition. This theoretical working paper separates epistemic burden, professional identity, status threat, and governance concerns rather than treating opposition as evidence of jealousy. A small additive model distinguishes discovery-label-invariant formal validity from workload and utility. Eight Lean-checked propositions establish conditional workload relations, the possibility of overload, and the non-identification of latent motives from aggregate opposition. Public primary sources provide context but no representative psychological evidence. Deterministic synthetic examples illustrate the assumptions, and a prospective factorial study is proposed to test responses to source labels, verification packages, and credit rules. No participants were recruited and no empirical effects were estimated. The framework’s central contribution is an auditable separation of deductive consequences, documented positions, and hypotheses requiring evidence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The article discusses the current threats associated with the introduction of artificial intelligence technologies and social media activities in the learning environment of schoolchildren and students. Some directions for the development and training of critical thinking skills in modern technology are given, directions for improving the formation of digital hygiene and legal education in order to prevent destructive behavior are determined. The subject of the research is issues related to the influence of artificial intelligence on students of legal education institutions. The purpose of the work is to identify problems and develop recommendations in the aspect of the impact of modern technologies during the training of future graduates of lawyers. The methodology of the work was based on the provisions of modern psychology, pedagogy, and the concept of improving the educational process, in terms of developing learning with the active use of modern technologies. A set of scientific research methods was used: analysis and synthesis of conclusions from previously conducted psychological and pedagogical research in terms of studying the impact of artificial intelligence, as well as other modern information and telecommunication technologies in the context of training in legal educational institutions. The experimental work is related to the study of the behavior of law students and high school students in the context of studying the influence of artificial intelligence on them while actively using the capabilities of modern information and telecommunications technologies, including Internet resources, as a result of which a generalization of the accumulated material was carried out. The results of the work. The results obtained indicate the need to continue conducting additional research on the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on students, in a student and school environment in which modern information and telecommunications technologies are currently being actively used. The scope of the results. As a result of the research, the organizational and practical aspects of studying behavior in learning environments with the active use of artificial intelligence technologies by students of legal educational institutions are summarized.

Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are transforming how we design and build systems by increasing access to domain knowledge and by providing automation support to software engineering (SE). As implementation becomes less expensive through generalist SE agents, engineering effort shifts away from writing correct code and toward expressing, curating, verifying, and evaluating requirements. In this paper, we survey the state of the art in AI for requirements engineering (RE) research leading up to the transformation, before reviewing advances in LLMs. We survey two subsequent research areas: prompt programming, which treats LLM instructions as a program in SE vernacular, and generalist SE agents, which combine multiple LLM advances to yield semi-autonomous processes that complete SE tasks. Finally, we explore the future of requirements engineering along two axes: matters changing how we interact with requirements through the SE process, and matters changing how requirements are experienced by software developers and stakeholders more broadly, including end-users. This article aims to inform how RE researchers can navigate this transformation in the selection of future research priorities.

Explainability techniques are rapidly being developed to improve human-AI decision-making across various cooperative work settings. Consequently, previous research has evaluated how decision-makers collaborate with imperfect AI by investigating appropriate reliance and task performance with the aim of designing more human-centered computer-supported collaborative tools. Several human-centered explainable AI (XAI) techniques have been proposed in hopes of improving decision-makers' collaboration with AI; however, these techniques are grounded in findings from previous studies that primarily focus on the impact of incorrect AI advice. Few studies acknowledge the possibility for the explanations to be incorrect even if the AI advice is correct. Thus, it is crucial to understand how imperfect XAI affects human-AI decision-making. In this work, we contribute a robust, mixed-methods user study with 136 participants to evaluate how incorrect explanations influence humans' decision-making behavior in a bird species identification task taking into account their level of expertise and an explanation's level of assertiveness. Our findings reveal the influence of imperfect XAI and humans' level of expertise on their reliance on AI and human-AI team performance. We also discuss how explanations can deceive decision-makers during human-AI collaboration. Hence, we shed light on the impacts of imperfect XAI in the field of computer-supported cooperative work and provide guidelines for designers of human-AI collaboration systems.

BackgroundAs artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into the workplace, an important question concerns how employees respond when technological change is perceived as threatening rather than beneficial. Prior studies have examined several mechanisms linking AI awareness to employee attitudes and behaviors, but these mechanisms are often studied separately, limiting understanding of the broader psychological process underlying adverse employee reactions.ObjectiveThis study examines the mediating roles of job insecurity and psychological contract breach in the relationship between AI awareness and counterproductive work behavior (CWB).MethodsUsing meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM), we synthesized 45 independent studies involving 16,140 participants to test whether AI awareness influences CWB sequentially through job insecurity and psychological contract breach.ResultsBased on a pooled true-score correlation matrix, AI awareness was positively associated with job insecurity and CWB. Job insecurity was positively associated with psychological contract breach, which in turn was positively associated with CWB. The MASEM results indicated a significant but modest sequential indirect effect of AI awareness on CWB through job insecurity and psychological contract breach, alongside a substantial direct effect of AI awareness on CWB.ConclusionThe findings clarify how awareness of AI may contribute to negative workplace behavior. Job insecurity and psychological contract breach constitute a significant but relatively modest sequential pathway linking AI awareness to CWB. Because a substantial direct effect remained, additional psychological and organizational mechanisms are likely to contribute to employee responses to AI-related workplace change. These findings extend research on employee reactions to emerging workplace technologies.

Background: Saudi Arabia prioritises adopting artificial intelligence (AI) and Industry 4.0 for e-commerce and digital supply chains under Vision 2030, but implementation and alignment with diversification goals remain insufficiently synthesised in the literature. Objectives: The study examines the impact of AI and automation on digital supply chains, identifies drivers and obstacles in Saudi Arabia’s e-commerce, and assesses their alignment with Vision 2030’s sustainability and diversification goals. Method: Following preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, 30 peer-reviewed articles from 2020 to 2026 were reviewed from IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, using bibliometric and thematic analysis. Results: Findings indicate that AI accounts for 46% of variability in sustainable performance; hybrid machine learning models reduce demand prediction error by 8.58% and achieve forecasting accuracy of up to 92%. Saudi Arabia’s 99% internet penetration supports Internet of Things development, but organisational barriers such as cultural resistance, cost, and job displacement (0.51) dominate adoption challenges over technical issues. Conclusion: Digitalisation success relies on technical and social systems, including government training and cybersecurity, to leverage AI for economic diversification beyond oil under Vision 2030. Contribution: The study connects national strategies to digital transformation, emphasising cybersecurity, workforce training, and the integration of technical and social systems, acknowledging immersive and decentralised tech as foundational for next-generation IoT and e-commerce.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Is servant leadership really a Disneyland-inspired fantasy of sunshine, lollipops, and hand-holding that makes followers complacent and lowers the bottom line of organizations, as critics claim? This criticism overlooks that servant leaders, striving to bring out the full potential in followers, do not only give positive strokes but may also provide followers with critical feedback. To assess the role of critical feedback in mitigating the flaws of servant leadership raised by critics, this study introduces tough love, the delivery of criticism with a positive tone and clear intent to help recipients overcome their deficiencies. We hypothesize that the relationship between servant leadership and key outcomes, such as follower performance, is strengthened the more servant leaders provide followers with tough love. We contend that tough love is appreciated by followers, solidifies relationships with their leaders, and helps them to grow through self-expansion. We reason that this growth benefits their work behaviors and attitudes. With multi-source field data covering three points in time, controlling for positive and negative feedback and prior levels of dependent variables, tough love is shown to moderate relations between servant leadership and both in-role performance and organizational citizenship behaviors, with mixed results for creativity and turnover intentions.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This paper explores the enduring power of storytelling in film and critically examines the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on creative processes within the film industry. Utilizing the Creative Cognition Framework and the Csikszentmihalyi’s Systems Model of Creativity, this study investigates how AI tools influence both generative and exploratory cognitive processes in film storytelling. A qualitative methodology, combining a comprehensive literature review with thematic analysis of questionnaire responses from 20 film and multimedia students at the University of Abuja, Nigeria, reveals nuanced insights. Findings indicate that AI significantly augments creative processes by enhancing efficiency, facilitating idea generation, and streamlining production tasks. However, respondents consistently emphasize AI's limitations in replicating human emotional depth, cultural understanding, and originality, advocating for a hybrid human-AI collaborative approach. The paper contributes to the understanding of human-AI collaboration in creative domains, highlighting opportunities for innovation while reaffirming the irreplaceable essence of human artistry in storytelling.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research by expanding investigators’ capacity to examine complex information, identify unrecognized relationships, generate hypotheses, and develop innovative solutions to scientific challenges. This article examines the relationship between human scientific expertise and artificial intelligence, emphasizing AI’s computational capabilities alongside the importance of human judgment, methodological rigor, and scientific accountability. Drawing upon peer-reviewed research involving molecular biology, materials science, pharmaceutical discovery, autonomous experimentation, and human–AI collaboration, the investigation demonstrates how computational intelligence can extend scientific inquiry beyond the limitations of conventional research methods. Attention is given to AI-assisted knowledge synthesis, interdisciplinary discovery, hypothesis generation, and the identification of solutions within multidimensional research environments. The article evaluates concerns regarding algorithmic bias, hallucinated information, intellectual originality, research integrity, and the reliability of computationally generated conclusions. It argues that the legitimacy of AI-assisted research should be determined by evidentiary accuracy, methodological transparency, reproducibility, and independent verification rather than the technological origins of research assistance. Ultimately, the article concludes that artificial intelligence does not diminish the intellectual authority or responsibility of human researchers but can amplify their investigative capabilities. The integration of human expertise and computational intelligence represents an emerging scientific paradigm capable of accelerating discovery, broadening research participation, and expanding the boundaries of human knowledge.

documents.abstract: Since 2018, the STEM education landscape has been reshaped by rapid technological change, persistent inequities, and the global pandemic. This chapter reviews global progress in research, policy, and practice, highlighting international strategic frameworks and the transformative impacts of COVID-19 and artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on lessons from various interventions, this chapter concludes with an evidence-based vision for the future of STEM that prioritizes equity, sustainability, and systemic coherence across global learning ecosystems.

This study explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with smart grid systems to enhance renewable energy utilization and intelligent mobility. It highlights the transition from centralized power systems to decentralized, data-driven energy networks supported by IoT, big data, and advanced communication technologies. AI techniques such as machine learning and predictive analytics enable accurate demand forecasting, efficient energy management, and grid stability. The research also examines challenges in renewable integration, including intermittency and storage limitations, and presents AI-based solutions. Furthermore, it emphasizes the role of electric vehicles and vehicle-to-grid systems in achieving sustainable mobility, ultimately contributing to resilient, efficient, and environmentally friendly energy ecosystems.

The increasing use of generative AI (genAI) across cultural and (re)creative sectors is indisputable in contemporary times. Within the EU, these systems are classified as “general-purpose AI” models (Recital 99 of the Artificial Intelligence Act – AI Act) and are expected to deliver a wide range of economic and societal benefits, as affirmed in Recital 105 of the Act. Yet, significant concerns have emerged regarding their potential impact on individuals, civil society, and democracy. In the cultural domain, genAI technologies are widely employed to generate outputs often perceived as original. However, scholarly debate has increasingly highlighted the risk that their widespread diffusion may lead to a form of cultural impoverishment – understood as the depletion of cultural pluralism and diversity of artistic expression resulting from the pervasive use of these systems and their underlying architectures, as well as, ultimately, an increasing standardization of the outputs of the algorithmic creative process. These systematic risks are not merely social or political but also carry significant legal implications. The potential effects of genAI on freedom of (artistic) expression and cultural pluralism may, in fact, infringe upon fundamental rights enshrined in international human rights charters. Yet, the role of legal scholarship in addressing such risks remains uncertain. A promising conceptual instrument for tackling this issue is the notion of systemic risk, recently introduced in two key pieces of EU digital legislation: the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the mentioned AI Act. This article examines the advantages and limitations of employing this concept to address the risk of cultural impoverishment. The analysis focuses primarily on the EU legal framework, with particular attention to the AI Act, while adopting a functional and comparative perspective, given that the principal challenges stem from US-based AI systems. It also situates the inquiry within the broader dynamics of the data economy, specifically the logic of knowledge capitalism. The article begins by exploring the potential impacts of genAI on cultural pluralism and artistic expression, assessing whether these may with time culminate in cultural impoverishment – or even a transition toward cultural monism, marked by the predominance, in all the cultural productions, of a single mainstream culture. It then analyses whether EU digital regulation is equipped to subsume such phenomena within the legal category of systemic risk.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In 2023, 18% of American adults said they had ever used ChatGPT. By early 2026, that number was 44%. AI adoption in the workplace has been even more remarkable. According to Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index, 75% of knowledge workers were already using AI at work, with nearly half having started within the preceding six months. We did not vote to hand over drafting, summarizing, fact-checking, and even thinking to these systems. There was no big decision. Just a free chatbot, a looming deadline, and a prompt that saved twenty minutes. Then another, and another... Regarding this serious issue, I was drawn to a new paper quietly posted on SSRN last September by Professor Vuong Quan Hoang. It gives this slow handover a name: the Correction Freeze Problem (CFP). His question is simple: can a system think it is fine while it is drifting away from reality, and stay that way not because it is lazy or lying, but because the very way it corrects itself makes staying blind the rational choice? The paper answers yes. In four different ways. And when any of those ways meets a world that rewards going along, the drift becomes a trap that is much harder to escape than it was to fall into. To grasp these insights, you don't need the math. Simply because you've lived it.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Physical activity is an essential requirement for a healthy life. And physical activity should be sustained for a long term. While there is a broad understanding and agreement that it is needed, per WHO report (2022) nearly 50% of Indian adult population does not do the required physical activity. There can be several reasons including COVID impact, Work from Home, Digital service revolution, etc. contributing to this inactivity. While these factors have a negative impact on physical activity, individual (intrinsic) factors do have an impact on behaviour of physical activity. There are several theories relating to human behaviour. This paper focusses on what theories can be leveraged to enable people to develop sustained physical activity behaviour. Two important psychological theories – Self Determination Theory (SDT) and Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) are established theories in human behaviour domain. Components of these 2 theories and to what extent they relate to sustained physical activity behaviour are discussed in this paper. 25 participants of a physical activity program were interviewed. They were able to develop sustained physical activity. Researches in this area – SDT and TPB, empirical studies provide valuable insights into application of these theories to develop programs / interventions (by health care, government, fitness centres, families, peers, friends). Programs may need to be customized by agencies to enhance intrinsic motivation and behavioural intent that will have a positive impact on bringing the desirable change in individuals. Programs will need to apply other components of SDT and TPB as appropriate such that it contributes to the cause.

This experiential exercise adapts the traditional Oxford-style debate format to channel the pervasive student usage of Generative AI (GenAI) into a productive tension, inviting students to sharpen their critical reasoning, rhetorical discernment, and real-time argumentation skills. Students use GenAI to help them develop initial arguments and counterarguments, then engage in real-time rebuttals where they must think independently, respond to novel challenges, and adapt beyond their GenAI-prepared materials. This approach transforms GenAI from a potential crutch into a pedagogical catalyst that reveals the irreplaceable value of audience engagement, human judgment, critical thinking, and adaptive reasoning. The exercise forces students to scrutinize reasoning (both GenAI’s and their own) against standards of logic, clarity, and relevance, by confronting GenAI-assisted arguments and then dealing with spontaneous counterarguments. The exercise has been implemented in undergraduate strategic management and business ethics classes. It can also be valuable for higher-level courses and for other course subjects.

BACKGROUND: Obesity's global rise has outpaced the effectiveness of "one-size-fits-all" prevention and treatment strategies. The promise of precision medicine lies in addressing the etiological and biological diversity of obesity and transforming it into actionable endotypes. OBJECTIVES: In a narrative review, we analyze "obesityomics," looking at the contributions each omics layer makes to understanding and managing obesity. The areas we evaluate are genomics (heritability, polygenic risk, and monogenic forms), epigenomics (development and environment imprinting), transcriptomics (tissue-specific programs of adipose, liver, muscle, and hypothalamus), proteomics (signaling networks and adipokines), metabolomics and lipidomics (fuel partitioning, lipotoxicity, and metabolic inflection points), and microbiome science (metabolites, host-microbe interactions, and microbial ecology). Our domain-by-domain (single-omics) approach demonstrates how disease taxonomy, causal pathways, and biomarkers can be refined and targeted therapeutically. DISCUSSION: We argue that "obesityomics" is a pragmatic approach to aligning omics modalities to the right questions at the right time, not a wholesale merger of datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI)-including machine learning and deep learning-should be used in conjunction with quality control, feature selection, modest data integration, and obesity intervention prediction. Among the key challenges in managing sensitive multilayer data are harmonization, standardization, reproducibility, equitable representation, and governance. The translation priorities include prospective studies related to patient-centered outcomes, biomarker panels that are clinic-ready, interoperability standards, and cost-effectiveness evaluations. CONCLUSION: The review maps concrete steps to assist people with obesity in making better choices by identifying what each omics domain excels at and introducing a brief AI perspective.

Risk management is one of the fundamental components of a company's success, whatever its sector of activity. This paper reviews the work done in the field of risk management, both traditionally and by integrating Artificial Intelligence. It highlights the way in which risk management was solved in the traditional way, discussing methods and approaches and citing the limitations of traditional risk management. It also outlines research into the integration of Artificial Intelligence into risk management in the various phases of the risk management process. Based on the open literature published in the various journals in the field of risk management, the stages of the risk management process are the result of human judgment, which may identify risks or, for psychological or/and social reasons, may not, so human subjectivity influences the risk identification phase and all phases of the risk management process. To reduce this subjectivity and to reduce human contact in this phase, our article proposes a model based on Artificial Intelligence that attempts to identify risks and treat them in order to reduce or eliminate existing risks.

documents.abstract: The global semiconductor industry has become a strategic pillar of the digital economy and mainly supports the artificial intelligence technology, cloud computing, advanced manufacturing, and modern electronic devices. Forecasting international semiconductor trade flows is therefore essential for governments, researchers, and policymakers. In this paper, we propose TradeGraph, a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that combines Graph Attention Networks (GAT), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) and GraphSAGE through an adaptive gated fusion mechanism for bilateral trade flow prediction. This research used the BACI international trade database. First, we analyze the structural evolution of the global semiconductor trade network and identify its major trading communities. Then, we develop a hybrid GNN model that we compare with three baseline GNN architectures under a temporal train-validation-test split, to predict the semiconductor trade flow. Experimental results demonstrate that TradeGraph achieves the best predictive performance and exhibits lower variability across multiple independent runs. Our results reveal that the global semiconductor market is characterized by a limited number of major trade blocs and suggest an increasing importance of Asian economies in the global semiconductor trade network over the study period. These findings demonstrate the potential of hybrid Graph Neural Networks for analyzing and forecasting complex international trade networks.

Digital transformation changes the competencies organizations need, so competency matrices must be rethought as tools linking business needs with human resource (HR) development. This study synthesizes how the competency-strategy matrix is transformed in the digital era. A systematic literature review (SLR) following PRISMA 2020 was applied to journal articles from Google Scholar, Garuda, Neliti, and Scopus. The matrix evolves through administrative, strategy-linked, and digitally adaptive stages. Digital transformation shifts competency demands toward digital, data, and behavioral skills, while technologies such as enterprise systems and artificial intelligence bring efficiency but also the risk of dehumanization. The study proposes an integrative framework and a research agenda.

The convergence of robotics and precision agriculture (PA) marks a transformative shift in modern farming practices aimed at enhancing productivity and ensuring long-term sustainability. This chapter explores the integration of advanced robotic systems into agricultural operations to address critical challenges such as labor shortages, resource inefficiency, and environmental degradation. It provides an in-depth analysis of various robotic applications, ranging from autonomous tractors, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) (drones), and robotic arms to artificial intelligence (AI)-driven monitoring systems that contribute to site-specific crop management, precision irrigation, pesticide application, and harvesting. The chapter emphasizes how robotics, when combined with sensor technologies, data analytics, and machine learning (ML), enables real-time decision-making and optimized farm management. Furthermore, it discusses the socio-economic and environmental benefits of adopting robotic solutions, along with the barriers to implementation and future research directions. By offering a comprehensive overview, this chapter aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers committed to the advancement of sustainable and high-efficiency agriculture through robotics.

This study investigated the extent of utilization, challenges, and strategies for transforming mathematics teacher education through artificial intelligence (AI) and digital innovation in Colleges of Education in Gombe State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study adopted a descriptive survey design involving 75 stakeholders (21 administrators and 54 mathematics lecturers) drawn by census sampling from Colleges of Education in Gombe State. Data were collected using a validated 30-item questionnaire (Cronbach alpha = 0.84) and analysed using mean, standard deviation, and independent-samples t-test at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that AI and digital tools are utilized to a low extent overall in mathematics teacher education (cumulative mean = 2.70), with only dynamic geometry software and mobile learning applications utilized to a high extent. Ten challenges were affirmed as significant, most notably inadequate ICT infrastructure, high cost of digital devices and data, and lack of institutional policy on AI use (cumulative mean = 4.06), while resistance to change and data-privacy concerns were not strongly endorsed as major challenges. Nine strategies were identified as needed to enhance AI and digital integration, most notably reliable electricity and internet infrastructure and regular capacity-building training for lecturers (cumulative mean = 4.05). The t-test results showed no statistically significant difference between administrators' and lecturers' perceptions across extent of utilization (t = 1.05, p = 0.30), challenges (t = 0.55, p = 0.58), and strategies (t = 0.60, p = 0.55). The study concludes that despite low current utilization, stakeholders strongly endorse both the barriers and the pathways toward meaningful AI-driven transformation of mathematics teacher education, and recommends deliberate infrastructural investment and sustained capacity building as priority interventions.

Large language models (LLMs) are commonly associated with the distributional hypothesis, according to which (1) semantic meaning is grounded in distributional patterns of linguistic context, and (2) knowledge of cross-linguistic distributional correspondences allows for successful translation. This paper rejects the first claim as a causal inversion: linguistic distributions reflect patterns arising from meaning-making practices rather than constituting their source. At the same time, it accepts the second claim, arguing that translation -human or machine - can succeed without requiring access to meaning or reference. Knowledge of interlingual distributional correspondence and their inferential organization may be sufficient for translation. The paper develops an ecological-enactivist perspective, according to which reference and meaning are grounded in agent-environment interaction and stabilized through action-grounded concepts, forms of world-involving cognition that current LLMs do not possess.

This study aimed to provide a comprehensive systematic review of research published in peer-reviewed scientific journals in Arabic and English between 2022 and 2026 that investigated the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot, and others, on translation and translation education among professional translators, translation students, and faculty members. The study used the PRISMA 2020 framework for systematic search, screening, and documentation, and employed a thematic analysis approach based on the model developed by Braun and Clarke. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria to 24 initial records, the final analysis included 18 studies. The findings revealed that the most significant benefits of using generative AI tools included improved efficiency and productivity, reduced time to complete translation tasks, support for post-editing processes, improved certain translation quality indicators, and the promotion of self-directed learning and the development of professional competencies among translators and students. At the same time, the results identified several challenges, most notably terminological accuracy issues, difficulties handling cultural and idiomatic expressions and local dialects, risks associated with overreliance on intelligent systems, and ethical concerns involving privacy, transparency, and professional accountability. The review also showed that the impact of generative AI varies by text type, specialized domain, and the assessment tools used. In addition, it highlighted limited evidence available concerning the Arabic language, particularly in areas such as legal translation, idiomatic expressions, and local dialects. This study contributes an interpretive framework based on the concept of “Gains and Pains” to explain generative AI’s dual impact on translation and translation education. The findings conclude that generative AI does not fully replace human translators; rather, it serves as a supportive tool that reshapes translators’ professional roles toward reviewing, verifying, and evaluating outputs. Accordingly, the study recommends integrating generative AI tools into translator training programs within clear pedagogical and ethical frameworks. They should also include post-editing, critical thinking, and output-verification skills, and support further specialized applied research in the Arab context.

Autonomous AI agents can perform increasingly consequential actions on behalf of users, creating a need for human oversight that is proportional to the potential risk of each action. This paper presents TrustGuard, a lightweight and interpretable risk-aware human oversight framework for AI agents. TrustGuard automatically evaluates proposed actions using five factors: privacy risk, financial risk, data modification risk, irreversibility risk, and external impact. Each factor is scored from zero to five, producing a total score from zero to twenty-five. Based on the score, actions are classified as Low, Medium, or High Risk and mapped to autonomous execution, user confirmation, or human approval. A prototype was implemented using Python and Streamlit to demonstrate the framework. The rule-based analyzer was calibrated using 120 development scenarios and subsequently evaluated on a held-out pilot set of 30 new scenarios. TrustGuard correctly classified 27 of the 30 test scenarios, achieving 90 percent accuracy. The results demonstrate the potential of transparent risk-based oversight while also identifying limitations in detecting some security-sensitive and privacy-sensitive actions.

documents.abstract: Tumor antigens provide the molecular interface between malignant transformation and host immunity, but their biological significance is determined by more than their molecular existence. Antigen clonality, abundance, processing, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) presentation, dendritic-cell function, T-cell recognition, spatial immune organization, and the surrounding tumor microenvironment (TME) collectively determine whether an antigen becomes immunologically visible and therapeutically actionable. Across cancer progression, tumor-cell antigenic states and the TME undergo reciprocal selection: immune pressure can eliminate highly visible clones while favoring antigen-loss variants, HLA defects, immune exclusion, suppressive myeloid and stromal states, and treatment-resistant populations. Recent single-cell, spatial and three-dimensional imaging, as well as immunopeptidomic studies show that this evolution is heterogeneous across tumor regions and anatomical compartments rather than a uniform linear process. This review therefore advances an antigen-TME co-evolution framework linking primary tumors, lymphatic and nodal immune compartments, systemic dissemination, distant metastatic niches, therapy, minimal residual disease, and recurrence. It critically evaluates the strengths and limitations of the classical immunoediting model; compares melanoma, breast, colorectal, lung, prostate, sarcoma, and virus-associated cancers according to antigen source, clonality, presentation competence, immune architecture, and dominant therapeutic bottleneck; and examines clinical translation through checkpoint blockade, cellular therapy, vaccines, antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, immunopeptidomics, and computational antigen prediction. Particular attention is given to the gap between predicted peptide binding and verified presentation or immunogenicity, the need for longitudinal rather than single-biopsy profiling, and the requirement for prospective validation of artificial-intelligence models. The central conclusion is that tumor antigens become clinically meaningful only when antigenic state and microenvironmental context are assessed together, providing a more rigorous foundation for precision cancer immunotherapy.

Artificial intelligence is reshaping governance and economic systems worldwide, yet many countries in the Global South remain dependent on technologies, infrastructures, and governance models produced elsewhere. This dependency reflects deeper patterns of digital colonialism, including data extraction, reliance on foreign cloud systems, and limited capacity to shape AI on local terms. Grounded in African empirical evidence with broader application across the Global South, this paper argues that universities are critical but overlooked institutions in efforts to strengthen AI sovereignty. While governments, firms, and civil society face persistent capability gaps, universities hold mandates that position them to build research capacity, cultivate technical and governance expertise, and coordinate innovation ecosystems. Drawing on political economy and higher education scholarship, the paper develops the Capability–Alignment–Impact (CAI) Framework to explain how universities can contribute to autonomous AI development through three pathways: strengthening foundational knowledge; improving coordination across government, industry, and civil society; and translating expertise into societal impact. The paper concludes by outlining practical implications for policymakers, development agencies, and university leaders seeking to support sovereign AI ecosystems in the Global South.

The article examines the possibilities of using generative artificial intelligence in teaching the discipline “Engineering and Computer Graphics” in the design of robotic models for the processing industry. The feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence models into the design process of robotic systems as a means of developing spatial thinking, graphic competence, design skills, and digital skills of agricultural university students is substantiated. It is established that modern generative systems (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Claude, DALL·E, etc.) support all stages of educational design, from developing technical specifications and generating product concepts to creating drawings and three-dimensional models, visualizing designs, preparing technical documentation, and analyzing possible design solutions. A methodology for using generative artificial intelligence in the educational project “Design of a Robotic Manipulator” is proposed. The methodology is based on the principles of project-based learning, STEM education, the competency-based approach, and the use of CAD systems. A structural model for integrating generative artificial intelligence into the process of graphic training has been developed. It includes the stages of problem formulation, concept generation, sketch creation, three-dimensional modeling, preparation of design documentation, and expert evaluation of the finished product. It is demonstrated that the use of generative AI contributes to increasing students’ motivation, developing engineering thinking, fostering digital literacy, and reducing the time required for routine operations in the design of robotic models.

documents.abstract: The article examines main aspects of artificial intelligence use in master's degree teaching of Linguistics and Pedagogical Education spheres. Artificial intelligence is currently being actively integrated into the educational process, transforming traditional formats into a more dynamic one: it quickly analyzes information, adapts materials on demand, systematizes and structures information, and personalizes educational content. In this article, the authors emphasize the competent training of future specialists/qualified personnel who will possess in-depth knowledge of the theory and methodology of teaching foreign languages, as well as skills in using innovative technological advances in professional teaching, and will be in demand in the future labor market. Based on the conducted research, the essence of using AI tools in the educational and linguistic environment is revealed, allowing for increased individualization and interactivity in the foreign language learning process. The modern education system is currently undergoing an active digital transformation, driven by the rapid development of information technology and artificial intelligence (AI). It was concluded that artificial intelligence can offer enormous potential for improving the quality of education, reducing the time and effort required by teachers, and facilitating the independent work of master's students. The obtained results allowed us to expand the scientific understanding of the use of AI in educational process and identify solutions for its application by higher education teachers in practical classes. The study materials will be useful for education and philology researchers and teachers improving the educational process.

Mapping an atomic structure to a compact set of geometric descriptors is an essential step in any machine-learning application to atomic-scale modeling. A powerful and widely used approach can be understood as a discretization of the histogram of pair distances, triangles, etc., which results in a hierarchy of symmetry-invariant atom-centered descriptors. Unfortunately, the lower rungs on this hierarchy (two, three, four-body clusters) were found to be incomplete, with symmetry-unrelated pairs of structures having exactly the same descriptors. However, all the "degeneracies" reported so far are resolved by considering larger clusters of neighbors to build the descriptors. We report examples of 3D structures that are indistinguishable even if one considers clusters of up to seven neighbors, and to arbitrary order when considering a practical level of discretization of the descriptors, discovered with the assistance of large language models. The key ingredients in their construction can be traced to results that have been known for decades in different communities: the model was able to find the references and recognize their significance for the problem at hand. We believe that this experiment exposes an extremely fruitful usage pattern for Artificial Intelligence in science: translating results between different communities and application domains, accelerating the process by which serendipitous discoveries in a field become breakthroughs in another.
